#7622. Brian Kilmeade and Dr. Kevin Roberts on the Stories That Forged a Nation

As the United States commemorates 250 years since its founding, Americans have an opportunity not only to celebrate the nation’s remarkable history, but also to rediscover the people, principles, and defining moments that made the American experiment possible.

In his new book, Uniting the States: Six Crucial Moments That Forged the American Miracle, Brian Kilmeade brings the early years of the U.S. to life through the stories of six Americans whose courage and conviction helped shape a fledgling republic. From John Adams’s defense of the rule of law and George Washington’s leadership in the Revolution to Thomas Jefferson’s Louisiana Purchase and James Madison’s stand against Great Britain, these pivotal moments reveal how a young nation confronted division, uncertainty, and extraordinary challenges.

Brian Kilmeade and Heritage Foundation President Kevin Roberts bring these lessons of great American leaders to the new generation. They explore the character, ideas, and leadership that forged the American miracle and consider what it will take to preserve that inheritance for generations to come.

#7621. Disability Discrimination and Allegations of AI Use in Student's University of Michigan Course Papers

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"[A]t this stage of the case, ... [plaintiff] plausibly pleads that [the university] discriminated against her by disregarding [her medial records] to find that she used AI when the writing style of the course papers could have resulted from her disabilities."

From Doe v. Regents of Univ. of Mich., decided yesterday by Judge Laurie J. Michelson (E.D. Mich.):

Plaintiff Jane Doe filed this lawsuit against the University of Michigan and several individual defendants after she was disciplined for her alleged use of AI to write course papers. Plaintiff, who has generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), maintains that the "tone, meticulous structure, [and] stylistic consistency" of her writing can be misinterpreted as AI. Unconvinced, Defendants sanctioned Plaintiff with disciplinary probation and required her to rewrite those course papers and write a reflective essay. After challenging that discipline without success, Plaintiff filed suit, asserting claims under the due process clause, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), and the Rehabilitation Act (RA). …

This dispute unfolded last fall when Plaintiff was an undergraduate student in Great Books 191, a classical studies course at the University of Michigan. The class was taught by Theo Nash, the course's graduate student instructor, and Basil Duffalo, the lead instructor. According to Plaintiff, Nash made public "statements reflecting a predisposition to assume AI misuse by students and to treat AI-related concerns as a core academic 'values' issue."

The issues at the heart of this case started when Nash filed an academic misconduct accusation with the Office of Student Academic Affairs (OSAA), indicating he was "immediately suspicious" Plaintiff had used AI to write a course paper. Plaintiff denied that accusation, "explaining that [her] disability-related writing traits could be misinterpreted as AI and should not be treated as proof of misconduct."

Plaintiff participated in a conference with OSAA and submitted materials supporting that position. Not long after, Nash filed a second misconduct accusation based on another paper written by Plaintiff. He attached "AI-generated comparison outputs created by prompting AI with [Plaintiff's] own outline and with instructor feedback." Before OSAA's involvement on this second accusation, Nash asked Plaintiff to meet. Plaintiff declined. In Plaintiff's telling, Nash "interpreted her declination as 'self-destructive' and a refusal of help." Plaintiff then went through the same OSAA proceeding for the second accusation. OSAA found Plaintiff responsible for both accusations and sanctioned her with disciplinary probation (notated on her unofficial transcript) and also required her to write a reflective essay.

Five days later, Nash filed a third misconduct accusation with OSAA for another paper written by Plaintiff. Plaintiff again submitted materials to OSAA including "written notices" "explaining that an NR grade was blocking degree requirements and graduation and that her transcript and future educational opportunities were being harmed immediately."

Before OSAA adjudicated the third accusation, Plaintiff filed a complaint with the Dean of the College of Literature, Science, and the Arts, and the University President's Office, "about disability discrimination, retaliation, harassment, and lack of procedural neutrality in the OSAA process." The University responded that Plaintiff could appeal OSAA's findings, which Plaintiff soon did. That same day, Plaintiff filed a complaint with the U.S. Department of Education and the University's Equity, Civil Rights, and Title IX Office (ECRT). OSAA, in turn, paused Plaintiff's appeal pending ECRT's review.

ECRT dismissed Plaintiff's complaint given her approved accommodations. With that decision complete, OSAA then issued the same misconduct finding for the third accusation. Plaintiff was also required to rewrite course papers for Great Books 191.

In Plaintiff's view, Defendants "treated disability-related traits and limitations as evidence of guilt and failed to apply disability-informed modifications in the academic integrity process." That led Plaintiff to file this lawsuit. Plaintiff brings her claims against the Regents of the University of Michigan ("the University") and several individual defendants in their official and individual capacities, including Nash and Duffalo, and Sean Edgerton and Christine O'Neil from OSAA. …

The court held the individual defendants were entitled to qualified immunity as to the due process claim, since any alleged constitutional violation wouldn't be "clear to a reasonable" government official; an excerpt:

Based on the allegations in the complaint, Nash (and Duffalo) were faced with course papers that resembled the use of AI. Plaintiff has provided no case suggesting it would be "clear to a reasonable" university instructor that using AI-detection software to analyze that writing and bring an academic misconduct allegation as a result of that analysis would violate a student's procedural due process rights….

And the court rejected the due process claim against the institution:

[Plaintiff] was advised of the accusations that she used AI to write course papers. Her sanctions included disciplinary probation notated on her unofficial transcript, a requirement to write a reflective essay, and rewriting course papers. But before they were imposed, Plaintiff was given opportunities to provide her side of the story, including that her GAD and OCD caused writing traits that could be mistaken for AI. She provided medical documentation to OSAA, and OSAA expressly considered that information in its decision. In effect, Plaintiff "admits that [s]he received exactly the due process [s]he requested."

Pivoting from the process provided, Plaintiff maintains that OSAA's sanctions "rested on Nash's self-confirming AI comparison outputs." That argument is unsupported by Plaintiff's allegations and exhibits. Again, they show that OSAA considered Nash's conclusions against Plaintiff's explanations. And when forming its decision, OSAA even credited information Plaintiff provided that sufficiently disputed one of Nash's conclusions … ("In your evidence you indicated that the idea of the 'rat king' was something talked about in your discussion section which we were able to confirm.")….

All told, "[w]hen assessing whether an academic dismissal constituted a due process violation, '[a] court must 'show great respect for the faculty's professional judgment' and may not 'override' that judgment 'unless it is such a substantial departure from accepted academic norms as to demonstrate that the … committee responsible did not actually exercise professional judgment.'" The parties rely on this academic-dismissal standard even though this case involves assessing whether a disciplinary probation notation on an unofficial transcript and a requirement to write a reflective essay and rewrite course papers constitute a due process violation. But based on the allegations in the complaint and attached exhibits, the Court cannot find that Defendants departed from accepted academic norms or failed to exercise professional judgment.

The court also rejected plaintiff's claims that the university failed to accommodate her disability, and that the university retaliated against her for asserting rights related to her disability. But it allowed plaintiff's intentional disability discrimination claim to go forward:

[Plaintiff] describes the discrimination theory in her response brief as follows:

Nash's public statements reflecting a 'paranoid' predisposition to find AI everywhere, combined with his decision to file three successive accusations grounded in the very writing traits Plaintiff's clinicians had warned would be misinterpreted, and OSAA's decision to sustain those findings while disregarding the clinical record, collectively support an inference of intentional discrimination.

For their part, Defendants do not advance significant argument on this claim[, arguing instead that] … "With respect to the denominated claims of 'discrimination,' the Complaint does not actually contain any allegations of direct (i.e., intentional) discrimination. For that reason and to that extent, Claims I and II should be dismissed." … Yet Plaintiff maintains that her discrimination claims "are supported by allegations of intentional … discrimination." …

There can be no dispute that Plaintiff pleads Nash's "paranoid' predisposition" to find AI, and her submission of clinical evidence explaining why, given her disabilities, her writing style might be misinterpreted as coming from the use of AI. It is also true that the exhibits Plaintiff attached to her response brief that the parties are treating as integral to the allegations in the complaint, show that OSAA reviewed her clinical record.

But at this stage of the case, the Court must accept as true Plaintiff's allegation that OSAA disregarded the medical evidence. In other words, although Defendants considered and/or reviewed Plaintiff's medical records, she plausibly pleads that they discriminated against her by disregarding them to find that she used AI when the writing style of the course papers could have resulted from her disabilities.

Plaintiff further alleges that she provided Nash and Duffalo with information about her disability accommodations such that they were on notice of her disabilities. She pleads that she rejected Nash's request to meet with him outside of OSAA. Taking these allegations as true and drawing reasonable inferences in Plaintiff's favor, that rejection likely resulted from the effects of her disabilities, including difficulty with "live verbal defense, rapid processing, and adversarial questioning."

Indeed, that is seemingly why "Plaintiff requested that OSAA permit her to present her defenses in writing rather than through additional live Zoom proceedings, consistent with her disability-related limitations." But Nash, according to the allegations, interpreted Plaintiff's rejection of his request to meet as "self-destructive" and then followed up with another misconduct accusation to OSAA. Accepting these allegations as true, combined with Plaintiff's allegations about Nash's "'paranoid' predisposition" to find AI, Plaintiff plausibly pleads a claim for disability discrimination under the ADA/RA.

NEXT: Today in Supreme Court History: November 10, 1975

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. #7620. Former state official charged with tampering bar exam results

The former executive director of the Arkansas Supreme Court’s Office of Professional Programs faces 65 felony counts after an investigation found “extensive irregularities” with bar exam results from 2020 to 2025, according to the state supreme court. (Image from Shutterstock)

The former executive director of the Arkansas Supreme Court’s Office of Professional Programs faces 65 felony counts after an investigation found “extensive irregularities” with bar exam results from 2020 to 2025, according to the state supreme court.

During the course of at least eight bar administrations, Nancie Givens, who left her post in February, took points from some bar examinees and assigned them to others, moving some candidates to a minimum passing score, according to a Thursday press release.

In at least one case, according to the state supreme court, Givens changed a score of an examinee who earned a passing score to a failing one.

A criminal investigation initiated in April by the Arkansas State Police and the FBI found that 11,400 files were deleted or unavailable, most including bar examinee applications, profiles and exam score sheets that the Office of Professional Programs was required by the Arkansas Supreme Court’s rules to retain for 25 years, according to the press release.

“If these allegations are true, these actions constitute an unprecedented breach of public trust,” according to the press release.

The state supreme court, state and federal authorities are working to recover deleted and missing data, analyze the impacted test administrations, and determine the full scope of the crime, according to the press release.

The “vast majority” of Arkansas bar examinees who had been notified that they passed “did, in fact, pass the exam” according to the press release, but those impacted by the misconduct will ⁠be notified “as soon as possible upon definitive confirmation of their status,” the Arkansas Supreme Court said.

For the July 2025 bar exam, 244 people took the bar exam in Arkansas, with a 70% pass rate, according to the National Conference of Bar Examiners.

#7619. School Districts' Negligence and Nuisance Claims Against Social Media Companies Rejected by California Court of Appeal

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Some short excerpts from the long decision Thursday in Social Media Cases (San Diego Unified School Dist. v. Meta Platforms, Inc.) by California Court of Appeal Justice Anne Richardson, joined by Justices Elwood Lui and Stephen Goorvitch):

In recent years, various plaintiffs have brought numerous legal claims against social media companies. In this opinion, we address only two causes of action—negligence and public nuisance—in the context of the laws of California, Florida, Washington, and Rhode Island, brought by school districts…. Plaintiffs generally claimed Defendants created a "mental health crisis" among their students that harmed Plaintiffs by disrupting their educational mission, requiring them to spend more money and staff time to address student mental health and discipline, and causing students to vandalize their property….

We acknowledge the serious allegations of mental health harms experienced by many students and the impact of those harms on Plaintiffs' schools and student bodies…. [But the relevant precedents] establish that these plaintiffs cannot proceed under the legal theories and factual allegations they have pled….

Here, Plaintiffs allege they suffered three general kinds of harm: (1) "incur[ring] significant financial costs" to address the youth mental health crisis allegedly created by Defendants' platforms; (2) "frustrat[ion] [of their] pedagogical mission" in diverting staff time and resources from education to counter the disruptive effects of the crisis; and (3) property damage inflicted by students. In part V., we conclude Plaintiffs' allegations their missions were frustrated do not state a cognizable negligence claim, and in part VI., we conclude Defendants have immunity from liability arising from Plaintiffs' alleged property damage. {Plaintiffs do not allege Defendants directly damaged their property; instead, they allege Defendants' platforms influenced students to vandalize school property because the platforms showed them so-called "challenge videos," created by third parties, that encouraged vandalizing school property. The trial court determined [47 U.S.C. § 230] provided Defendants immunity from liability arising from the challenge videos. We agree.}

That leaves Plaintiffs with only alleged financial harms …. The crux of the negligence causes of action is the applicability of the so-called "economic loss rule." … "… In general, there is no recovery in tort for negligently inflicted 'purely economic losses,' meaning financial harm unaccompanied by physical or property damage" [even as to foreseeable economic losses -EV]…. "[A]ssume[ ] a defendant negligently causes an automobile accident that blocks a major traffic artery such as a bridge or tunnel. Although defendant would be liable for personal injuries and property damage suffered in such an accident, it is doubtful any court would allow recovery by the myriad of third parties who might claim economic losses because the bridge or tunnel was impassible." …

Nuisance suits are generally either public or private. "[A] private nuisance is a civil wrong based on disturbance of rights in land[,] while a public nuisance is [based] upon an interference with the rights of the community at large."

"Nuisance has been described as an 'impenetrable jungle'" that "'mean[s] all things to all people'" and "'is incapable of any exact or comprehensive definition.'" Thus, while nuisance is often defined broadly, many courts have limited its scope in practice. For example, the Washington Supreme Court expressly limits nuisance claims "to property infringement [and] threats to health and safety." Some of our fellow Courts of Appeal have prohibited bringing products liability claims in the guise of public nuisance actions.

Such limits are often imposed because of a concern that "nuisance 'would [otherwise] become a monster that would devour in one gulp the entire law of tort.'" In the products liability context, "'[a]ll a creative mind would need to do is construct a scenario describing a known or perceived harm … that can somehow be said to relate back to the way a company … makes, markets and/or sells its non-defective, lawful product or service, and a public nuisance claim would be conceived and born.'"

The trial court concluded Plaintiffs failed to adequately plead public nuisance because the harms alleged to have befallen individual student users of Defendants' platforms did not amount to a public nuisance, even when "considered collectively." While our analysis may differ from the trial court's in some particulars, we ultimately agree Plaintiffs' efforts to state a cause of action for public nuisance fail under the laws of California, Washington, and Florida….

California nuisance is broadly defined by statute as "[a]nything which is injurious to health, including, but not limited to, the illegal sale of controlled substances, or is indecent or offensive to the senses, or an obstruction to the free use of property, so as to interfere with the comfortable enjoyment of life or property, or unlawfully obstructs the free passage or use, in the customary manner, of any navigable lake, or river, bay, stream, canal, or basin, or any public park, square, street, or highway, is a nuisance."

Public nuisance is defined by statute as "one which affects at the same time an entire community or neighborhood, or any considerable number of persons, although the extent of the annoyance or damage inflicted upon individuals may be unequal." "[P]ublic nuisances are offenses against, or interferences with, the exercise of rights common to the public." "It is [the] community aspect of the public nuisance … that distinguishes it from its private cousin," and makes it suitable "to protect the quality of organized social life."

Perhaps because of those broad definitions, our Legislature has codified who has standing to bring a public nuisance action. Certain persons may bring an action for public nuisance when it is "specially injurious" to them or when their property is "injuriously affected or [their] personal enjoyment is lessened."

By contrast, a "public body or officer authorized thereto" can bring an action to abate a public nuisance. And the State or designated county or city officials, in their representative capacities, can bring an action limited to abatement under Code of Civil Procedure section 731. San Diego's action, however, is not limited to abatement, but seeks damages for harms allegedly caused by the nuisance. The only recognized exception to the limitation on remedy is that a public entity may seek damages when it sues in its role as a property owner.

While San Diego makes a number of arguments related to its public nuisance theory, some of which have divided our fellow Courts of Appeal, we need not parse them in detail because San Diego failed to adequately allege its standing to bring a public nuisance cause of action….

San Diego first argues it has standing under Civil Code section 3493. That statute expressly allows "[a] private person" to bring a public nuisance action…. [G]overnment entities are not "private person[s]" for purposes of section 3493….

In the alternative, San Diego argues it may bring a public nuisance cause of action pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 731. That statute provides "[a]n action may be brought by any person whose property is injuriously affected, or whose personal enjoyment is lessened by a nuisance, as defined in Section 3479 of the Civil Code," and damages may be recovered. …

San Diego's complaint did not adequately plead its property was "injuriously affected" or its "personal enjoyment [was] lessened" by the alleged nuisance of Defendants' platforms…. Rather, the complaint's focus throughout its 286 pages is on the "unprecedented mental health crisis" among students and its disruption to schools' public educational mission…. Any connection to property here is abstract at best.

Accepting San Diego's position would convert virtually any personal injury affecting a property owner into a nuisance. For example, consider a homeowner whose son breaks his leg in a car accident with a negligent driver, rendering him unable to use the stairs in the home. Even if the homeowner must spend time and resources to help her son navigate the home, she has no nuisance cause of action against the driver on the ground the driver interfered with her use and enjoyment of her property….

Because all Plaintiffs' causes of action fail for the reasons discussed, we do not consider whether they are entirely barred by section 230 and the First Amendment to the United States Constitution….

Jonathan H. Blavin and Victoria A. Degtyareva (Munger, Tolles & Olson), Paul J. Watford, Bailey J. Langner, David P. Mattern and Geoffrey M. Drake (King & Spalding), Mark W. Mosier, Ashley M. Simonsen and Christian J. Pistilli (Covington & Burling), and Ashley W. Hardin, George A. Borden and Neelum J. Wadhwani (Williams & Connolly) represent defendants.

#7618. Twelve crime movies where justice actually prevails

It’s an incredible week. Progressive democratic candidates SWEPT the elections. In the biggest congressional win of the last five decades, we flipped a bunch of red states, and elected smart, community-and-inclusion-minded leaders who prioritize healthcare, the environment, minority rights, and livable conditions. Abdul El-Sayed! Jon Ossoff! James Talarico! Gina Hinojosa! Annie Andrews! Melat Kiros! Amy Acton! Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia became the first Black woman governor in the whole country!!! It’s an incredible moment in American history, a true victory over the narcissistic, bigoted, murderous regime in power currently.

It’s been a great week, so let’s keep the party going. If you’re looking for something that will get you fired up for justice, this weekend, may I recommend one of the following twelve classic movies.

These are political/legal/journalism movies about moments that Truth and Goodness and Fairness prevail. And you know what? Many of them are based on a true story!

This is not a comprehensive list, just the movies I thought of in my post-election euphoria. Happy watching… and power to the people!

Frank Capra’s Mr. Smith Goes to Washington is about RAMPANT GOVERNMENT CORRUPTION so yes it’s a crime movie, and yes it’s very topical. Next slide, please.

Ah yes, the classic story about how two Washington Post reporters exposed the Watergate scandal and brought down Richard Nixon. O, for a president with Richard Nixon’s sense of decency. And that’s saying something.

Every single person in Congress should watch this movie, this weekend.

The whole point of America is for everyone—ANYONE—to have a fair trial.

Sure, the truth can be adjusted… but it will also eventually come out!

Sarah Polley’s adaptation of Miriam Toews’s somber, charged novel about women in a Mennonite community who collectively gather in the hayloft of a farm to address the systemic sexual abuse perpetrated upon them by the men of the colony (and to vote on what they should do about it), is riveting. It is a true ensemble film and feels often like a play—a brave and compelling story about women who decide not to accept what they are told they must.

The fight is worth it!!!!! Fight for the future!!!!!

If you haven’t, you should really watch this engrossing heist-ish thriller adaptation of Andreas Malm’s groundbreaking nonfiction book. Malm’s book argues that that peaceful protests have proven themselves ineffective in stopping the widespread annihilation of the earth and its inhabitants by climate change, and the only thing that can make any real change is property damage. The film follows a group of young people (mostly early 2os but a couple people around 30) as they band together with a specific mission: destroying a new oil pipeline that has been built in Texas. They all have different reasons for coming to this decision, but their effort will be both a symbol of resistance and a real, practical hindrance to the environmental ravaging posed by the pipeline.

This is a good movie, that constructively, caringly reenacts Jodi Kantor and Megan Twohey’s investigation into the crimes of Harvey Weinstein.

Remember when The Washington Post published the Pentagon Papers? A great moment for justice, a great moment for truth in America.

The TRUE story of the legal researcher who made a corporation pay for its toxic environmental destruction and public health dangers.

#7617. 7 novels where Americans in Paris solve mysteries

“Paris is so very beautiful that it satisfies something in you that is always hungry in America,” wrote Ernest Hemingway in a letter to his mother. The pull to Paris from across the ocean has always been strong. Since the 1800s Americans have traveled to the City of Light in search of artistic, intellectual, and personal freedom. They found better (but not perfect) racial equality, the mental and physical space to write or paint, affordable rent (in the good old days), cheap red wine, ethereal croissants, and very often romance.

The experiences of real-life Americans like Hemingway, Josephine Baker, Julia Child, and James Baldwin inspired a trove of fictional stories. In books, movies, and TV series these characters’ storylines often followed a similar trajectory. Once in Paris the Americans became more sophisticated, more assured, more themselves. Think of Frank Mulligan, Gene Kelly’s character in An American in Paris, Audrey Hepburn’s Sabrina, or the titular Emily in the Netflix hit Emily in Paris.

In the popular imagination, Paris is a place of joie de vivre, of pleasure. But, the rose-colored glasses through which we Americans often view the city also makes Paris an ideal setting for mysteries and thrillers. Who doesn’t love experiencing the frisson of danger lurking behind a pretty façade?

The main character in my new mystery novel The Foreign Correspondent’s Wife finds that very darkness in the City of Light. It’s 1949, and Kat Kelly is a whip-smart reporter who’s run out of the profession when men return home from the war. She comes to Paris with Charlie, her foreign correspondent husband, and enrolls in culinary school, eager to make a fresh start. But when one of her classmates, a former GI, is brutally murdered, she becomes obsessed with solving the crime, soon suspecting that the killing has its roots in the Nazi Occupation of Paris during World War II.

Like Kat, most American characters in mysteries or thrillers set in Paris have much to learn from the city. But, often, they bring a uniquely American perspective to whatever shenanigans they find themselves embroiled in—a can-do attitude, a refusal to take no for an answer, a moxie that makes them the ideal person to ferret out the truth.

Kat and Charlie join a long line of Americans starring in mysteries and thrillers set in Paris. Here are a few of my favorites.

No, this 2026 novel isn’t about the 2025 Louvre heist. But what timing! Piazza’s most recent page-turner features dual timelines, both revolving around the art of Vincent Van Gogh.

In the first, set in the 1990s, Emma is an American art student forced to clean apartments when her École des Beaux-Arts scholarship is canceled. Soon she gets drawn into the mysterious world of her employer, the disinherited matriarch of a stupendously rich—and potentially criminal—family of art dealers.

In the second, we follow Jo Van Gogh, the painter’s real-life sister-in-law as she struggles to build a market for Vincent’s work after his death. The stories braid together beautifully, and with fraud, assault, a soupçon of romance, and of course a heist, this one’s a real work of art.

The Maggie Hope series is anchored in World War II-era Britain, but in the seventh installment, the Massachusetts native finds herself in occupied Paris on a dangerous mission. The mathematician-turned-spy must discover the fate of both a fellow agent and her half-sister.

The narrative is teeming with fascinating historical details and real-life characters, but it never feels heavy-handed.The Paris Spy is a smart, fast-paced story that’s full of both action and heart.

The second entry in Pavone’s Kate Moore series finds Kate living in Paris with her family. She’s overseeing a sleepy CIA substation, attempting to shore up her flailing marriage, and planning dinner parties in an effort to fit in better with the other international moms.

When seemingly unrelated incidents flare up across the city—a bomb threat at a train station, a suicide bomber near the Louvre, an American billionaire spirited out of his apartment—Kate realizes that everything is connected and she may be the only person who can unravel the plot before it’s too late.

Packed with cameos from the city’s landmarks and biting asides, The Paris Diversion is the rare espionage thriller that’s as witty as it is twisty.

Mark Pryor, The Most Mysterious Bookshop in Paris

When Pryor launched the Hugo Marston series in 2012 with The Bookseller, his main character and our de facto detective was head of security at the U.S. Embassy in Paris. When his friend, an antiquarian bookseller, is kidnapped, Marston can’t help but pursue the case.

Nine books later and Marston has retired from the embassy to open a bookshop of his own. But when blackmail and murder come for a high-end chocolate maker located in an ancient Parisian chateau with a troubled history, Marston is drawn back into the city’s dark web of secrets.

While Black’s popular Aimée Leduc series wouldn’t make this list—Aimée may live in Paris, but she’s not a Yank—this spy thriller does. Set during World War II, Three Hours in Paris features Kate Rees, an American markswoman who is dropped into the Nazi-occupied French capital by the Brits with an assignment to assassinate Adolf Hitler on his visit.

When the plan falls apart, Kate must evade capture in a city teeming with danger while trying to figure out who betrayed her.

Colleen Cambridge, In the Spirit of French Murder

The fourth book in this post-World War II cozy mystery series is a gem. It finds American Tabitha Knight once again investigating a murder alongside her larger-than-life, food-obsessed pal Julia Child. This time, the victim is an elderly man who’s friends with Tabitha’s grandfather and his partner.

Eerie encounters with a medium, forays into dangerous parts of the city, and mouthwatering culinary descriptions keep this clever confection of a book moving at a brisk, entertaining clip.

Okay, this is cheating because the characters in this page-turner are Canadian, so North-American, but it’s too much of a favorite to omit. Number 16 in the Chief Inspector Armand Gamache series, which is mostly set in Quebec, this installment finds Gamache and his family in Paris on vacation. When his billionaire godfather is struck and gravely injured in a hit and run, Gamache realizes it was no accident.

The act of violence sparks a ticking clock mystery that sets the chief inspector and his son-in-law (and former deputy) Jean-Guy Beauvoir criss-crossing the city, unsure whom to trust and desperate to uncover the truth before it’s too late for their family.

Jenna Helwig is the author of The Foreign Correspondent, the food director at Real Simple, a five-time cookbook author, a culinary school graduate, and the creator of the Cookbookery Collective Substack. When she isn’t cooking or writing, she’s likely reading mystery novels, watching baseball, or planning her next travels. Jenna lives in Brooklyn, New York, with her family and adorable dog Pepper.

#7616. Former district attorney sentenced to prison in bribery scheme

Jody Owens, the former Hinds County, Mississippi, district attorney, at a legislative hearing in 2023. Owens was sentenced to more than three years in prison after being convicted of bribery. (Photo by Rogelio V. Solis/The Associated Press)

The former district attorney of Mississippi’s largest county was sentenced Thursday to more than three years in prison after being convicted of bribery.

Jody Owens, the former Hinds County, Mississippi, district attorney, was accused of soliciting $250,000 in bribes in exchange for awarding city contract bids to certain people in a scheme that also ensnared other city officials, the Associated Press reports.

“He took an oath to uphold the law, and yet he solicited $250,000 in bribes to rig what should have been a fair and open bidding system for city contracts,” said U.S. District Judge Daniel P. Jordan III of the Southern District of Mississippi.

In addition to his prison sentence, the court also ordered Owens to pay a $100,000 fine.

Owens ran for office as a criminal justice reformer, promising to focus on prosecuting violent crime while looking for alternatives to incarceration for nonviolent offenders.

“I can’t begin to tell you the shame I feel,” Owens said in court. “I betrayed myself, my family, my friends and my colleagues by my foolish and repugnant actions.”

#7615. New in Civitas: "The Blue Tsunami Threatens To Drown Originalism"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"Going forward, the path of advancing the conservative legal movement requires a political reorientation."

My new essay in Civitas tries to make sense of how the midterm election affects the broader conservative legal movement. Here is the introduction:

President Donald Trump's surprise 2016 election saved Justice Antonin Scalia's seat and perhaps the Supreme Court. Over the ensuing decade, Trump appointed scores of originalist judges at all levels of the judiciary and led a political movement that supported originalist state court judges and attorneys general. But that movement came to a screeching halt with the 2026 midterm election. Indeed, the blue tsunami, largely a referendum on Trump, threatens to drown originalism. In deep red states, conservative judges were washed off the bench. Also swept from office were conservative governors who appoint judges and attorneys general who litigate in those courts. Given the large Democratic Senate majority and unfavorable maps for 2028 and 2030, a Republican Senate with the votes to confirm originalist judges may not return until 2033 at the earliest. An entire generation of talent will be wasted. A necessary condition for a successful legal movement is a successful political party. Legal conservatives need to carefully reconsider the political circumstances best suited to defend the Constitution.

The conservative legal movement has always existed in conjunction and disjunction with the broader conservative political movement.  Certain long-term projects concerning the separation of powers and individual rights endure regardless of who is in office, but legal disputes arise with the exigencies of the day. The conservative legal movement will often, but not always, coalesce around current conservative political needs. Likewise, the conservative political movement will often, but not always, coalesce around the conservative legal movement. During two recent events, Justice Elena Kagan recognized this dichotomy. She observed that conservative members of the Supreme Court decide cases that are right "out of the playbook of the conservative legal movement," even as some of President Trump's policies suffer setbacks in the courts. Indeed, Trump has repeatedly expressed frustration that his appointees rule against him.

Many legal conservatives came to terms with voting for Trump in 2016 as a way to save the Supreme Court. Many more legal conservatives came around to Trump in 2020 based on his track record of appointing originalist judges--although I think that record is overstated. When Trump was on the ballot in 2024, some legal conservatives supported Trump for fear that Kamala Harris would pack the Supreme Court. But 2026 altered the calculus. Trump, and those candidates he endorsed, were routed in red states. Moreover, conservative judges and attorney generals were wiped from office. When the top of the ticket is no longer able to win elections, downballot judges and attorneys general do not stand a chance. Red states can only bleed for so long until they turn blue. A necessary condition for a successful legal movement is a political party that can produce viable candidates. Going forward, the path of advancing the conservative legal movement requires a political reorientation. The conservative legal movement can only survive if conservative lawyers are in public office to move the law. The blue tsunami cannot be allowed to drown originalism.

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

#7614. 5 mysteries that explore the darker sides of Dublin

Dublin is a city of many words. Of Nobel prizewinners and pub storytellers, never short of a thing or two to say. From the calligraphy of the Book of Kells to the modernism of James Joyce to the intricate interior worlds of Sally Rooney, Dublin’s literary heritage is long established.

But there’s a darker side to this city, a corrupt underbelly of money and power, a rich history of villains and anti-heroes. Here are some of my favorites.

From the queen of Dublin noir, this is a tense, atmospheric investigation into the murder of a family on one of Dublin’s ghost estates in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crash. Brianstown is built on the ruins of a faded seaside resort and it embodies all of the isolation and desperation so prevalent at the time.

It’s bleak and brutal and a searing indictment of a government that put the survival of its banks ahead of the welfare of its people. It’s also a grueling mystery that plays out to the very end.

This compelling exploration of the 1982 murders committed by Dublin socialite Malcolm Macarthur is both true crime and a fascinating dive into the mind of a convicted killer. After Macarthur was arrested at the then Attorney General’s home, an event that almost brought down the government, he spent forty years in prison.

On his release, O’Connell approached him in the street to talk about his life. The result is an insightful and unsettling study of a “highborn savage” so convinced of his own superiority that he will go to any lengths to blur the lines between truth and invention. As a bonus, The Book of Evidence by John Banville, shortlisted for the 1989 Booker Prize, is inspired by Macarthur’s story.

A whydunit it more than a whodunit, this is a masterful exploration of the motivation and morals of a group of private-school teenagers. When Conor Harris is kicked to death by three of his peers, the Dublin establishment is forced to look beyond its veneer of respectability for answers. A connected yet distant narrator deconstructs institutional entitlement, broken family dynamics and the moral decay that can hide behind money, old and new.

Inspired by real events, Bad Day in Blackrock is a scathing yet sometimes tender glimpse of a section of Dublin society still getting used to its newfound Celtic Tiger wealth.

Andrew Hughes, The Convictions of John Delahunt

This chilling historical thriller is based on the true story of a notorious Victorian murderer. When a lackluster Trinity student becomes a police informant, it’s not long before he’s looking for scapegoats for his own crimes. Delahunt starts to fabricate conspiracies and frame innocent people to claim government bounties until his greed and escalating moral decay culminates in a shocking, cold-blooded murder that scandalizes the entire nation.

Set among the taverns, tenements and alleyways of 1840s Dublin, and courtrooms that dole out their own twisted justice, this is an engrossing and vivid portrait of a city as sinister and corrupt as its amoral protagonist.

And if I may be so bold… In 1980s Dublin, outsider Lou Manson enrolls at the prestigious Highfield Manor to try and expose the school’s dark secret. But she soon discovers that the Highfield elite will go to any lengths to protect their own reputation—even when the consequences are fatal.

When We Were Silent is a propulsive and fiercely feminist exploration of power, corruption and retribution.

Fiona McPhillips is an Irish journalist, author, and screenwriter. In 2019, she started an MA in Creative Writing at Dublin City University, graduating with first class honours. Fiona's debut novel, When We Were Silent, was runner-up for the 2021 Crime Writers Association Debut Dagger. Fiona lives in Dublin with her three kids, two cats, and a dog.

#7613. Art, syrup, a legendary stone: Maxie Dara’s 3 favorite heists of the last century

Crime is a subject often synonymous with tragedy, with strife, with human suffering. But sometimes it’s also a little goofy.

I spent my first two books, A Grim Reaper’s Guide to Catching a Killer and A Grim Reaper’s Guide to Cheating Death, focused on the murder of it all. My search history probably has me on at least one watch list and I can give you a handful of creative ways to kill somebody with a glitter pen if you ask nicely.

But for my third dive back into my world of death with A Grim Reaper’s Guide to Living Twice, I decided to play against type and go for a silly little heist instead. And it turns out I’m not alone. It fact, it turns out recent history is full of silly little heists that take the concept of a crime and turn it into a certified shenanigan. From student hijinks to condiment capers, here are my top three favorite heists of the last century.

Come with me to my home nation of Canada, to my birth province of Quebec, where poutine is plentiful and everybody’s at least a little disappointed in your lack of French fluency. It also happens to be a hub of maple syrup production, though that feels like something of an understatement. According to The Canadian Encyclopedia, “In 2020, Quebec contributed 96.4 per cent of Canadian maple product exports.”

With all that sweet tree nectar flowing, it may come as no surprise to you (though it genuinely did to me) to learn that the province keeps a syrup stockpile in the form of the Strategic Maple Syrup Reserve. Think of it as a sort of Fort Knox, but instead of gold it’s filled with pancake toppings, which is way more appealing in my opinion. And I’m not the only one who thinks so.

Between 2011 and 2012, a group of sticky-fingered (sorry) Reserve employees decided to help themselves to the stock in order to sell it to other provinces and states. This slow-motion heist involved months of siphoning maple syrup out of heavy barrels. The thieves would then either replace their loot with water or leave the barrels empty. Unfortunately for the robbers, there’s a bit of a difference between an empty barrel and one filled with syrup—a six-hundred-pound difference, in fact.

When an inspector for the organization in charge of the Reserve tried to climb up a stack of these supposedly heavy barrels only for one to nearly topple under his weight, he became just a smidge suspicious. Sure enough, a subsequent investigation found that around three thousand tonnes of maple syrup had been stolen, its value a staggering $18 million.

The investigation also uncovered a crime ring comprised of syrup industry insiders, from truck drivers to sugar shack workers, who had rented a separate space in the same warehouse as the Reserve so they could perpetrate their crimes unnoticed. Though my favourite fact about this entire case is that a maple syrup black market exists, and the ringleader of the operation, Richard Vallières, had already been a part of it long before this heist. Some criminal underworlds just sound more delicious than others, you know?

Kids these days, with their music and their haircuts and their schemes to steal back ancient symbols of Scottish heritage.

It’s Christmas in 1950 and four Glasgow University students have decided to crank their youthful rebellion up a notch. While other twenty-somethings are sleeping off hangovers or opening presents with their families, Ian Hamilton, Gavin Vernon, Kay Matheson and Alan Stuart are plotting to retrieve the Stone of Scone.

Also known as the Stone of Destiny, the roughly three-hundred-and-thirty-six-pound block of red sandstone had been an important part of Scottish coronations for hundred of years before King Edward I stole it for England during the 13th century. During its long history the stone was imbued with rich legends, connecting its heritage all the way back to the first king of Scotland and making it an important national symbol. South of the border it continued to be used in coronations, this time siting beneath each English monarch as they were crowned, but its importance to Scotland remained.

Centuries after its initial theft by King Edward I, the four plucky students decided to reclaim the stone in an act of national pride. The group drove south and waited until midnight to steal the Stone of Scone from where it now lay in Westminster Abbey.

With Kay on guard duty, the three men tried to hoist the stone to freedom, but it broke in two during their attempt. Ian took the smaller piece while Gavin and Alan took the larger and fled in a separate car. Back with Kay, Ian soon found himself in the crosshairs of a passing officer, but in an Ocean’s Eleven-like twist, the students disguised their heist as a youthful makeout session and managed to get away.

The story only gets more wild from there, with the stone halves finding themselves hidden under floorboards and buried under a campsite before they were eventually reunited. And while it did end up returning to England after the students were caught, the Stone of Scone was given back to Scotland in 1996, and none of the young thieves faced legal consequences for their actions.

The Louvre is no stranger to an entertaining heist. In 1911, a man called Vincenzo Peruggia dressed as a museum worker and snatched the Mona Lisa in broad daylight. Unfortunately for the Louvre but very fortunately for schadenfreude fans everywhere, the museum art minister was on holiday at the time and before he left he had apparently insisted, “don’t call me unless the Louvre burns down or the Joconde [French for Mona Lisa] is stolen.”

Fast forward just shy of a hundred years and this same level of absolute tomfoolery was on display again. In 2025, two men dressed as construction workers, hoisted themselves up to a museum balcony using a furniture lift and stole €88 million worth of French Crown Jewels in under eight minutes. Though the culprits were eventually caught, the heist will live on in infamy for both its devious efficiency and the frankly top tier memes it inspired.

Maxie Dara is a writer and actor from Ontario, Canada. She has been a freelance journalist focusing on the local arts and culture scene for more than five years, with bylines in publications such as Hamilton Magazine and Beyond James, among others. She is also a two-time award-winning playwright, taking home the Best of Fringe award at the 2017 Hamilton Fringe Festival for the musical comedy This Is Not a Musical: The Musical! and the 2020 Torpedo Prize for her play Alone Together, a pandemic drama. Maxie knew she wanted to be a writer at the age of seven, when she first fell in love with the written word. She also wanted to be a mermaid but has mostly focused on the writing side of things.

#7612. ‘ER’ and ‘The Pitt’ are similar enough for lawsuit to move forward, appeals court says

Actor Noah Wyle attends an event for HBO’s “The Pitt” at the David Geffen Theater on June 9, 2026, in Los Angeles. (Photo by Phillip Faraone/Getty Images for HBO)

A unanimous California appeals court on Wednesday found that medical TV shows ER and The Pitt have enough similarities that a lawsuit alleging that The Pitt is an unauthorized rebranded version of ER can move forward.

A three-judge panel from the Second District Court of Appeal in California ruled that the trial court judge correctly rejected a motion to dismiss the case brought by the widow and estate of ER creator Michael Crichton.

However, the panel dismissed actor Noah Wyle, who starred in both shows and produces The Pitt, as a defendant, along with two other producers who worked on both series.

The Pitt is an HBO Max series depicting a real-time day in the life of a Pittsburgh emergency department. It has won two Emmy Awards for best drama for its first two seasons and two Emmy Awards for Wyle for best actor, according to a story by the Associated Press.

#7611. The Queens Public Library system is being held for ransom

In a bizarre turn of events, on Wednesday November 4th, New York City’s Queens Public Library (QPL)  system (which operates 66 branches), experienced an attack on its online networks by a hacker. The entire system is offline, and is being held for ransom.

According to the QPL, all branches remain open, but online networks are down, resulting in disruptions to the library website, on-site computers, check-out and return machines, wi-fi, the library’s mobile app, and all digital media services.

It has not been disclosed what or how much the hackers are asking in return for releasing the system. It is also unknown who is behind the ransomware attack.

QPL CEO Dennis Walcott told Gothamist, “Unfortunately, it’s part of the world that we live in right now. So the Queens Public Library is a victim of the type of world that we’re living in, where people are launching cyber attacks against various types of entities, large corporations, and now Queens Public Library.”

His remark highlights the absolute strangeness of the events… the QPL is hardly a “large corporation.” In fact, it’s a very small nonprofit. It’s not even New York’s largest library system. The NYPL, which services Manhattan, the Bronx, and Staten Island, operates 92 locations. (For those wondering, the Brooklyn Public Library system operates 62 branches.)

But also… it’s a library system! It’s whole business is to provide widespread access to books, additional literary and media resources, internet access, printing services, education opportunities, and community and children’s programming to people. FOR FREE. What the hell type of jerk goes after a library system, especially a library system in one of the most ethnically and linguistically diverse areas in the world? (As a Queens native and huge QPL fan, but also just a person who thinks books are good, I’m furious.)

Walcott also noted that it is currently unknown if user information has been compromised.

However, QPL users can still check books in and out manually (it is a library, after all). So, analog tech has saved the day.

Stay tuned for more updates, and long live libraries!

#7609. Will an ability to hold federal officers accountable survive this term?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

At a time when there is a desire to hold ICE agents accountable for their constitutional violations, the Supreme Court might be poised to eliminate the only way to hold them civilly liable under federal law.

By way of background, if state or local officers violate the Constitution, they can be sued under a federal statute, 42 U.S.C. Section 1983. But no federal law authorizes suits against federal officers for constitutional violations. Rather, the ability to sue a federal government officer for money damages comes from a 1971 Supreme Court decision, Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics. There, the court said that it would allow a cause of action for money damages under the Fourth Amendment even without a federal statute authorizing it.

Nevertheless, for decades, the Supreme Court has refused to extend or even apply Bivens to other violations of constitutional rights by federal officers, and several conservative justices have called for it to be overruled. Now, in Nielsen v. Watanabe, to be argued on Nov. 9, the court will again confront whether to allow a Bivens suit – and perhaps whether to end such claims entirely.

The underlying issue is about separation of powers: should the court provide a remedy for constitutional violations or is that entirely the province of Congress? But it also is about accountability: without Bivens, how can those who violate constitutional rights, including ICE agents, be held responsible and how can those injured be compensated?

Webster Bivens alleged that he had been subjected to an illegal and humiliating search by agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics. Bivens sought money damages as compensation for the harms he suffered. The court held that a federal law cause of action for money damages could be inferred directly from the Fourth Amendment. The majority, in an opinion by Justice William Brennan, emphasized that individuals whose rights have been violated should not be relegated to state law remedies, which might be inadequate or hostile to the federal constitutional interest.

In an important and often-cited concurring opinion, Justice John Marshall Harlan explained that the federal courts long have devised remedies for violations of federal law. Harlan said that it is essential that federal courts be able to provide such relief because “it is apparent that some form of damages is the only possible remedy for someone in Bivens’ alleged position. … For people in Bivens’ shoes, it is damages or nothing.” Harlan rejected the claim that the court violates separation of powers when it creates such a cause of action and remedy. In his view, the court is responsible for upholding and enforcing the Bill of Rights, and, hence, the judiciary need not wait for the legislature in order to act.

Chief Justice Warren Burger and Justices Hugo Black and Harry Blackmun dissented. Each wrote an opinion arguing that separation of powers means that Congress, and not the court, should create a cause of action for damages against federal officers. Black explained that “[s]hould the time come when Congress desires such lawsuits, it has before it a model of valid legislation, 42 U.S.C. §1983, to create a damage remedy against federal officers.” Similarly, Blackmun argued that “it is the Congress, and not this Court, that should act.”

For a decade after Bivens, the court applied and extended it. In 1979’s Davis v. Passman, the court allowed a Bivens suit under the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment for an equal protection claim. Congressman Otto Passman fired his administrative assistant, Shirley Davis, because he wanted a male to fill the position. In allowing the suit against the congressman, the court emphasized the judiciary's role in ensuring effective protection of constitutional rights.

And only a year later, in Carlson v. Green, the court allowed a Bivens suit for violation of the Eighth Amendment. A mother sued federal prison officials on behalf of her deceased son, claiming that he was the victim of gross inadequacies of medical facilities and staff, which caused his death and constituted cruel and unusual punishment. A remedy was available under the Federal Tort Claims Act; thus, the issue before the court was whether a Bivens suit should be allowed in light of this alternative. The court concluded that Bivens suits were a “counterpart” to the Federal Tort Claims Act because the act creates liability for the federal government and a Bivens cause of action permits recovery from federal officers themselves. The court found no indication that Congress intended for the act to preclude Bivens suits.

Since 1980, however, the court has not ruled in favor of a Bivens claim. In its most recent decision about Bivens, 2022’s Egbert v. Boule, the court noted that it had “declined 11 times to imply a similar cause of action for other alleged constitutional violations” and that “in all but the most unusual circumstances, prescribing a cause of action is a job for Congress, not the courts.”

Specifically, the court has held that that such claims are not allowed if there is a statute that precludes suits (in 2010’s Hui v. Castaneda), or that provides an alternative remedy even if it is inadequate (in 1988’s Schweiker v. Chilicky). It has precluded Bivens claims for those injured while in the military, even for egregious violations of their rights (in 1987’s United States v. Stanley). It has ruled that Bivens suits should be allowed only if they are on balance desirable and consistently has found that they are not (in 2007’s Wilkie v. Robbins, 2017’s Ziglar v. Abbasi, 2020’s Hernandez v. Mesa, and Boule). And it has precluded Bivens suits against private prisons that contract with the federal government (in 2001’s Correctional Services Corp. v. Malesko) and the guards employed by them (in 2012’s Minecci v. Pollard).

Based on this line of cases, the court in Egbert v. Boule stressed that recognizing a Bivens cause of action “is ‘a disfavored judicial activity.’” The court stated that

The court then laid out the framework for Bivens claims going forward. According to the majority, this should be guided by a two-step inquiry:

This is a test that puts a very strong presumption against recognizing Bivens claims.

Like Carlson v. Green, Nielsen v. Watanabe involves an Eighth Amendment claim for cruel and unusual punishment.The case involves a prisoner, Kekai Watanabe, who alleges that he suffered a broken tailbone when attacked by other prisoners that caused him excruciating pain and that a staff nurse, Francis Nielsen, denied him medical care. The court granted review as to whether the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit “erred [here] in recognizing a Bivens cause of action.”

Watanabe argues to the court that this case is governed by Carlson v. Green and does not seek to extend Bivens in any way. His brief states: “Watanabe asserts the same kind of violation of the same constitutional right by the same type of defendant in the same institutional setting pursuant to the same substantive standards as the plaintiff in Carlson. This is precisely the kind of claim this Court has long understood Carlson to encompass.”

In response, Nielsen argues that Bivens suits are strongly disfavored and that there are “significant factual differences such as the immediacy and severity of the harm alleged” compared with Carlson. But that is not all: Nielsen also expressly argues that “Bivens should be overruled” and that “Congress, not the judiciary, creates causes of action.”

The court could affirm the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit and allow a Bivens suit, saying that this is governed by Carlson. Or the court could distinguish Carlson, accepting Nielsen’s argument that there are sufficient factual differences between the cases, essentially limiting Bivens claims only for cruel and unusual punishment claims involving deaths. Or the court could overrule Carlson but not overrule Bivens.

Or the court could overrule Bivens entirely, which several conservative justices have advocated in the past.

The fundamental disagreement, as it was in Bivens, is whether it is the judicial role to provide remedies for violations of constitutional rights or whether that is just for Congress. The practical reality is that without Bivens suits, those whose rights have been violated – even horribly – are left with no recourse. In Hernandez v. Mesa, for example, a boy in Mexico was killed by shot fired across the border by a federal agent in Texas. The court’s rejection of a Bivens suit left no remedy at all.

In that case, and in many other situations, the Federal Tort Claims Act does not allow suits against the United States. Often there are not state tort remedies available either. To paraphrase Justice Harlan, for people in the shoes of many injured by federal officers, it is Bivens suits or nothing.

I would like to think that the reports of egregious constitutional violations by ICE agents, including killings, would cause the court to realize the importance of Bivens suits and to not end such causes of action. That is what makes Nielsen v. Watanabe so important.

Erwin Chemerinsky is the Dean and Jesse H. Choper Distinguished Professor of Law, University of California, Berkeley School of Law.

#7608. Of mistletoe and murder: 7 holiday mysteries set in the past

Mysteries set during the weeks leading up to Christmas are some of my favorites, and I know I’m hardly alone in loving a good holiday read. There’s just something about the sights and sounds of merriment juxtaposed with the increasingly dark and cold nights that make for a mystery that is that much more fun than one set in any other time of the year.

This is especially true for historical mysteries, in my opinion. For instance, in Murder of a Merry Gentleman, the fourth installment of my Lady Petra Inquires series set in Regency-era England, I set the mystery of a bachelor gentleman’s death in the ballroom of the famed Almack’s Assembly Rooms during the fortnight (i.e., two weeks) before Christmas.

Possibly helped by the lack of modern technology, sometimes the absence of modern lighting, and occasionally the dangers of period-correct clothing, all the little contradictions that give a mystery with a Christmastime setting such an fascinating ambience made it all the more fun for me to write, and I think makes holiday whodunits set in the past all the more enjoyable to read.

Here are seven historical mysteries I’ve especially loved that are all set during the holidays, where the festive season gives as much to the whodunit as the plot, no matter what the time period.

Setting: New York, 1932.  After Grace Verlander, the assistant who keeps Macy’s department store running smoothly, receives a note from Santa Claus that claims he’s been sent a death threat, she ramps up security around the annual Thanksgiving Day Parade. Yet when a dead body turns up on a parade float, Grace must use all the secrets she knows about the store to help uncover a killer and keep Macy’s reputation shining.

Rhys Bowen, The Twelve Clues of Christmas (Her Royal Spyness, book 6)

Setting: Scotland and England, 1933.  When Lady Georgie escapes the dreadfully cold Scottish winter to help play hostess at a holiday party in the village of Tiddleton-under-Lovey, she doesn’t expect a series of murders to be part of the season. And when they start following the theme of a well-known Christmas carol, it’s up to Georgie to find the culprit before the twelve days turn even more tragic.

Jess Armstrong, The Devil in Oxford (Ruby Vaughn mysteries, book 3)

Setting:  Oxford, England, 1922. American heiress Ruby Vaughn is hoping to spend a quiet Christmas in Oxford when she reluctantly agrees to accompany her octogenarian employer, Mr. Owen, to an antiquities exhibition with a mysterious past.

But when the discredited scholar who collected the artifacts turns up dead, and an old friend of Ruby’s asks for her help, Ruby will be pulled into an investigation into the dark world of antiquities that may turn out to be more dangerous than she ever imagined.

Dianne Freeman, A Christmas Guide to Family and Murder (Countess of Harleigh mysteries, book 9)

Setting:  Norfolk, England, 1900. Frances Hazelton—the American-born and widowed Countess of Harleigh—and her still-new husband George travel to the Norfolk estate of her sister-in-law Fiona to enjoy the Christmas holiday.

Yet when the aftermath of a terrible storm finds the local (and possibly disreputable) doctor dead in a nearby field, Frances and Fiona will unearth many a secret in their quest to find a killer and restore the Christmas spirit to both her family and the local village.

James R. Benn, The Phantom Patrol (A Billy Boyle WWII mystery, book 19)

Setting: Paris, 1944. With France only recently liberated, Captain Billy Boyle, and former Boston cop working as a special investigator for General Eisenhower, is sent to Paris. After discovering a rare piece of art and connecting it to a French network of Nazi sympathizers and art smugglers who might be aided by a member of the British Army, Billy races to hunt down the culprit, taking him directly to the frontlines of the Ardennes Forest and what will be come the deadly Battle of the Bulge.

Katharine Schellman, Murder at Midnight (Lily Adler mysteries, book 4)

Setting: Hertfordshire, England, 1816.  When widow Lily Adler visits the family of her late husband in Hertfordshire for Christmas, she finds herself reunited with her friend Captain Jack Hartley and his younger sister, Amelia, who has recently become the subject of scandalous gossip.

When a wealthy gentleman is found dead after a snowstorm, it’s Amelia who is suspected, and it’s up to Lily to uncover the truth and clear Amelia’s name before the girl’s reputation is tarnished forever.

Charles Finch, The Fleet Street Murders (Charles Lenox mysteries, Book 3)

Setting: London, 1866.  Christmas for gentleman sleuth Charles Lenox means celebrating his engagement to his dear friend Lady Jane. That is, until the murders of two journalists brings Lenox into a new investigation, and a secret is revealed that casts doubt on his future with his fiancée.

As he splits his time between London and the northern town of Stirrington, where he is running for Parliament, Lenox is drawn into a complex case that mixes politics and murder, bringing death and danger closer to home than ever before.

Celeste Connally is the USA Today bestselling author of the Lady Petra Inquires series, an Agatha Award nominee, and a former freelance writer and editor. Her mysteries are set in Regency-era England and feature a headstrong heroine, a feminist spin, and as many equestrian scenes as her plots and editor will allow. She delights in giving her mysteries a good dose of romance, too, and a few research facts she hopes you’ll find as interesting as she does. Passionate about history and slightly obsessed with period dramas, what Celeste loves most is reading and writing about women who don’t always do as they are told.

#7607. 2 BigLaw firms face proposed class actions over cyber breaches

In newly filed proposed class action lawsuits, plaintiffs are alleging that cyberattacks at Baker McKenzie and Squire Patton Boggs led to exposure of their personal information. (Image from Shutterstock)

In newly filed proposed class action lawsuits, plaintiffs are alleging that cyberattacks at Baker McKenzie and Squire Patton Boggs led to exposure of their personal information.

The complaint against Baker McKenzie was filed in the Northern District of Illinois on Wednesday. According to Reuters, Baker McKenzie said last week a cybercriminal in August “socially engineered two of our users” to obtain a limited number of files, but that “there was no independent malicious access to our system.”

Squire Patton Boggs disclosed its breach in October, saying it involved “an unauthorized third party obtaining a limited set of information from the firm,” Reuters reports.

The complaint against Squire Patton Boggs was also filed Wednesday but in the Northern District of Ohio.

Neither law firm responded to requests for comment from Reuters.

#7606. Virginia Trench on psychological thrillers and the dark sides of motherhood

There were ear-splitting screams. Bites. Lies of all shapes and sizes. Existential crises. And, it goes without saying, a lot of blood. Motherhood has all the raw materials for a good thriller.

Certainly not me—I was about to get a crash course, though. I was blissfully unaware of just how real my work would become once I had a newborn and second-degree tear in tow. I never expected to bring some of the most visceral aspects of my work home with me. But when my daughter arrived, all that went out the window.

From the moment we left the hospital, both of us exhausted, well out of our depth, and wearing diapers, something felt broken in me. (The baby, to be clear, was absolutely perfect).

I, by contrast, was nothing like the serene, softly smiling, well-lit mothers of Instagram. I felt more like a light-averse creature sharing more in common with feral raccoon than a human woman. I craved everything I couldn’t have: silence, rest, solitude, the home phone number of the anesthesiologist who messed up my epidural. A girl can dream—a mother can just tough it out.

As our new reality set in, everything I’d ever heard about motherhood started to seem like an elaborate, generations-long lie. But then, I reasoned, that couldn’t be the case. Surely, I must be the ugly, defective exception to the rule that childbirth and motherhood are the most beautiful, natural things in the world.

I gritted my teeth and waited for a switch to flip. Not not fantasizing about smashing the rocking swing with the annoying music, I did my best to fake it. I was desperate for the *alleged* biologically hardwired maternal peace to settle over us, to give my daughter the mother she deserved…and to prove the lactation consultant wrong—I wasn’t already failing because I’d given up on breastfeeding pretty much immediately.

Goodbye, Instagram moms. Hello, Nightbitch.

Sleepless night after shapeless day into the next sleepless night, I sank into a quicksand isolation, anger, and panic that came in bone-deep waves. Sure, I’d heard of postpartum depression, courtesy of delicately worded waiting room posters. I’d heard of the “baby blues,” a term was popularized by a man decades before American women could open their own bank accounts, receive paid maternity leave, or easily access contraception.

This experience was something else entirely, something huge, hungry, and raw. I used to love exploring those dark corners of human psychology. Through fiction, it was safe, easy to do from a creative distance. But that distance had vanished, and I found myself submerged in the extreme emotions that fuel stories I had no desire to live firsthand. The more I tried to escape those feelings, to remind myself how lucky I was and of the many privileges I have, the thicker my haze of shame became.

Out of sheer desperation, I tried something that seemed a little crazy at the time, even for a woman who heard phantom baby cries everywhere she went, including an empty Target bathroom. I evicted The Happiest Baby on the Block from my nightstand and replaced it with Rachel Yoder’s Nightbitch.

I faced the scary, socially unacceptable thoughts head-on. I nodded vigorously as I read. I started writing again. I gave voice to the emotional exhaust that followed me around like a swarm of black flies. And little by little, this brought me back from the brink.

In those pages, I finally, finally, found someone willing to level with me about the dark side of mothering.

As I tore through Yoder’s novel, I breathed in the unflinching honesty like fresh air. And after what I can only describe as the most isolated period of my life (despite rarely being alone), I could have lifted up Nightbitch like Simba in the Lion King.

To some, a twisted tale of rage and supernatural transformation might seem like an odd place to look for someone who gets you. Those people probably haven’t had to catch tiny human vomit with their bare hands or scrape diaper material from under their fingernails. For me, it was healing. It was therapy for the price of a hardcover—that eventually led to actual therapy. It was someone else, okay, fine, a fictional character, but still, validating everything so much of the world seems determined to silence.

Nightbitch was the gateway to more dark tales. It became an unexpected path back to a part of myself that got lost somewhere in the process of creating life and nesting the crap out of the former guest room. More than that, once I started reading thrillers again, I did so with new, narrowed eyes.

Psychological thrillers are a powerful channel for female rage, and the mom of it all adds fascinating layers to that rage. It’s hard not to occasionally lose your shit when (almost) everything is your fault.

Freudian psychology, direct ancestor of the manosphere, if you ask me, laid the groundwork to blame mothers for the behaviors and even the crimes of their children—especially their sons. We wonder: if a serial killer had just been nurtured properly, might innocent lives have been spared? Culture-defining classics from Psycho to Carrie feature the consequences of dangerous mothering, and audiences point the proverbial finger accordingly.

For that matter, is there anything more frightening than a bad mother? Sharp Objects and Verity terrify readers not just because of their villains’ psychosis, but their fundamental wrongness, their choice to harm, rather than nurture. That goes against nature, doesn’t it? After all, violence is supposed to be a man’s thing, isn’t it?

Most (all?) maternal attributes are fair game. A demanding career? Lack of career outside the home? An only child? Four under four? Homemade gluten free snacks? A Costco multipack or Cheez-Its?

Nothing is safe. All that pressure is enough to make anyone snap. And in this genre, that’s a great place to start.

Open Best Offer Wins, All the Other Mothers Hate Me, or Little Fires Everywhere, and we see death by a thousand little judgmental cuts, some of which are self-inflicted by the main characters. And as their stories unfold, we can’t look away.

Because instead of simply swallowing the judgement and striving to meet those double standards, these women make all hell break loose. And, as I can attest, there’s something cathartic about seeing that happen on the page. Many mothers have met their version of Renate Kline, for instance, ultra-judgmental supermom of Big Little Lies, and we can’t very well face off in real life and tell her exactly what we think of her, so it’s all the more satisfying to watch Reese Witherspoon do it for us in the TV adaptation.

It’s no wonder this genre draws in so many readers—we can relate to the characters’ experiences, ideally minus the murders.

If a “right” formula for this, it has eluded me completely. Too much hinges on who did/didn’t sleep through the night, which appliances are whistling at me, and whether my three-year-old is in a self-declared Aurora/ Ariel or Maleficent/ Ursula mood. So, I gave up looking, and I’m a much happier, better writer for it.

But I will tell you one thing: it helps to not have photos of my children in my office, and I feel zero guilt about this. Do I have a framed tooth in honor of the twist in Sharp Objects? A black and white portrait of Agatha Christie? Also, yes. But no adorable kids, and that’s okay, especially when I’m drafting a murderous chase scene.

It probably sounds corny: but the literal separation was necessary, even if my home office is feet away from the nursery. The best I can do is give make the space I can for different facets of my identity, which now includes, but is not eclipsed by, motherhood. Sometimes that space feels tiny, like hiding the last Annie’s Bunny Cracker bag for myself to pair with a glass of pinot noir.

Sometimes it feels huge, the inspiration for entire second novel, for instance, in all its raw, unfiltered glory (plus one sociopathic con man). What could go wrong?

Virginia Trench is the author of Our Secrets Were Safe. She studied English at Vanderbilt University before earning an MA in secondary education at University of Colorado Boulder. When she’s not writing, she can be found exploring the Rocky Mountains, struggling on a yoga mat while her cat judges her, or devouring the latest crime novels. She lives in Colorado with her family.
