#7538. Justices consider when a constitutional rule is “previously unavailable” to prisoner

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday heard argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, a case about whether a Texas man on death row can bring a second federal post-conviction challenge to his sentence by arguing that, under updated psychiatric standards, he was found intellectually disabled and therefore cannot be executed.

Except in a few narrow circumstances, the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 bars prisoners from filing a petition for federal post-conviction relief challenging the grounds for their detention when an earlier petition has already been rejected. One of these exceptions is when such a claim relies on “a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable.” The other is if facts “underlying the [initial] claim” would show “by clear and convincing evidence that, but for constitutional error, no reasonable fact finder would have found the applicant guilty of the underlying offense.”

In 2007, Dexter Johnson was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death for his role in the double murder of 23-year-old Maria Aparece and 17-year-old Huy Ngo. Five years before his conviction, the Supreme Court held in Atkins v. Virginia that executing people with intellectual disabilities violates the Eighth Amendment. A defense expert at Johnson’s trial concluded that, under the diagnostic standards employed at the time, Johnson was not intellectually disabled. Following his conviction, Johnson filed an initial habeas petition and invoked Atkins to argue – unsuccessfully – that its protections should extend to people with mental illness.

In May 2013, while Johnson’s first federal petition was pending, the American Psychiatric Association published the DSM-5, a new edition of its diagnostic manual that deemphasized IQ cutoffs. Texas’ highest criminal court adopted this in 2018. In 2019, Johnson scored 70 on an IQ test, and an expert concluded he met the DSM-5’s criteria for intellectual disability. Johnson then filed a successive habeas challenge in the district court claiming that he could not be executed under Atkins. The trial court subsequently ruled that his claim (based on the later diagnostic criteria) had been “previously unavailable,” and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit affirmed that decision. The 5th Circuit denied rehearing, and Texas came to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the case in June.

At oral argument, Texas Solicitor General William Peterson told the justices that Congress “chose to allow new claims in these applications only in limited circumstances that do not include changes in the diagnostic standards for intellectual disability.” There is no “new rule” “previously unavailable” here, because Atkins was decided before Johnson “even committed his crimes,” Peterson said.

Justice Elena Kagan pressed Peterson on why the DSM “isn’t … part of the law?” She suggested that the DSM-5 effectively created “a kind of Atkins I and an Atkins II” – first, a rule barring the execution of people with intellectual disabilities, followed by a “substantive standard” defining what it means to be intellectually disabled. Kagan later described the Atkins standard as akin to a rule with a “big gap in it” where “the DSM comes and plugs it in and it becomes part of the legal standard.”

The justices further debated what it means for a rule to be “available.” Kagan suggested, based on prior precedent, that something is “not available to you” if it makes you “run into a brick wall.” “[I]f I was going to be [previously] laughed out of court,” she said, “then, really, the rule was unavailable to me.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson told Peterson that, as she understood AEDPA, Congress’ “policy choice was to give individuals one clear shot at bringing their constitutional claims.” Under Texas’ interpretation, she said, “Mr. Johnson will never get that opportunity,” which “seems like a really incongruous consequence.”

Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for her part, suggested that the outcome should turn on something like ripeness (whether a case is sufficiently developed for a court to decide). As she remarked to Peterson, “[i]f what we have said under Atkins is you cannot execute someone who is mentally ill, we have a certain way of determining that, and it doesn't become ripe until the DM-5 makes it ripe.”

Justice Brett Kavanaugh asked Peterson whether the court “could resolve this case solely on the new rule issue without addressing ‘previously unavailable.’” Peterson said it could, but that Texas was asking the court to decide the “previously unavailable” question.

On behalf of Johnson, Jeremy Schepers told the justices that “existence and availability aren’t the same thing.” Atkins existed, but Johnson’s claim – based on the change in diagnostic criteria – was not previously available. When the clinical standards for intellectual disability change, Schepers argued, “the Eighth Amendment’s protected class potentially changes as well. And in those rare circumstances, that can render a rule legally available for the first time.”

Justice Clarence Thomas was skeptical, asking, “Does Atkins ever stop being a new rule?” Schepers responded that Atkins “remains new now.” “What about Marbury v. Madison?” Thomas responded. Justice Amy Coney Barrett noted that when “Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone, that was new.” But “I don't think anybody would describe the telephone as new today.”

Kavanaugh pointed Schepers to a “friend of the court” brief filed by Louisiana and 21 other states, which argued that because the medical standards are “constantly evolving,” Johnson’s position is “a recipe for eternal Atkins claims and zero finality.” Schepers said that was incorrect, because a state prisoner gets “one opportunity to raise any claim,” and “so a prisoner could not raise a second Atkins claim.”

At one point, Justice Samuel Alito asked about a future edition of the DSM that “makes smaller changes” that “provide a greater opportunity for success.” Schepers said that claim would fail under the 5th Circuit’s reading, because “[i]t’s only a question of whether the claim had a possibility of merit before.”

Emily Ferguson, an assistant to the U.S. solicitor general who argued as a “friend of the court” in support of Texas, emphasized that it is “difficult to imagine Congress enacting a law that would allow the American Psychiatric Association, without independent action of this Court, to create a new rule of constitutional law.” She also noted that the court had made clear “states would be responsible for the method of determining intellectual disability,” and it would then make little “sense for there to be an available successive application anytime the relevant state had a new … supreme court case … or even a state lower court case that changed the framework that the state was using.”

Alito asked Ferguson whether the “Atkins rule” was “that a person may not be executed if the person has an intellectual disability that is regarded as such by medical professionals,” or if “it is that a person may not be executed if the person has an intellectual disability that can't be justified by the recognized purposes of punishment,” for which “the DSM would be evidence but not part of the standard itself?” Ferguson responded that the “latter formulation captures what … the Atkins Eighth Amendment rule was.”

Perhaps the most noticeable takeaway from oral argument was how subdued the justices were. The chief justice did not ask any questions, and no justice appeared to take up Johnson’s request in his brief that the court dismiss the case as improvidently granted (that is, decide that it was a mistake to have agreed to hear the case in the first place and not resolve it), as the court did last term in Hamm v. Smith, another Atkins case.

A decision is expected by late June but is likely to come earlier.

Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

Zach is the executive editor of SCOTUSblog.

#7537. Feds warn SCOTUS against handing over policing power for immigrant labor laws

The Roberts courtâs push to disarm the administration state could disrupt the Trump administrationâs ability to enforce penalties for companies violating rules around foreign worker programs.

WASHINGTON (CN) â The Trump administration begged the Supreme Court on Tuesday to uphold its ability to enforce worker protections for immigrant laborers.

In Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, the justices considered whether the federal government can impose penalties on employers who violate H-2A program conditions through agency proceedings instead of courts of law.

Unlike Article III courts, administrative law judges fall under the executive branch. About 2,000 of these judges work across 30 agencies; by comparison, about 900 judges work throughout the judiciary.

Sarah Harris, the principal deputy solicitor general at the Justice Department, said it wasnât possible to bring federal court cases for hundreds of violations each year, leaving the government open to massive underenforcement of the law. And she warned an adverse ruling could ripple through other public benefit programs across the government, such as Medicare and federal student loans.

âPlease tell us if we need to get legislative affairs on it right now because this will snowball,â Harris said. âPlease reverse.â

The H-2A program allows U.S. employers to bring foreign nationals into the country to fill temporary or seasonal agricultural jobs when domestic workers are unavailable. In return for bringing foreign laborers into the country, employers must agree to terms and conditions, such as satisfying certain minimum standards for working and living conditions.

Sun Valley Orchards in New Jersey obtained permission for 96 H-2A visas for foreign workers to pick asparagus and peppers from April to October in 2015. Along with 51 domestic workers, the immigrant laborers were expected to work 12 hours a day with only a single one-hour break.

Sun Valleyâs laborers lacked access to drinking water and clean bathrooms while on the job, and their living conditions werenât much better. Workers were housed in six bedrooms with 20 bunk beds per room, and the bathrooms were dirty and lacked sufficient hot water.

Several workers met with Sun Valleyâs owner to discuss the substandard provisions. Instead of addressing their concerns, the company gave them prefilled departure forms to sign, stating they were voluntarily leaving because of personal issues. The H-2A workers were subsequently laid off midseason.

The Department of Labor launched an investigation and determined Sun Valley violated the H-2A program requirements. An administrative law judge and the departmentâs Administrative Review Board affirmed the findings, ordering the company to pay over half a million dollars in civil penalties and back wages.

But an appeals court said the case had to be brought through the federal judiciary under the Supreme Courtâs recent ruling in SEC v. Jarkesy. The 2024 decision was part of the Roberts courtâs recent spate of rulings disarming the administrative state, a term describing the governing power of the federal government and its agencies.

Harris argued Jarkesy included an exception for public rights claims. She said the H-2A program qualified because it involved government-granted privileges.

âThe government is exercising its plenary immigration power on the employer’s behalf to grant aliens visas and allow them to stay and work for that employer,â Harris said.

During the first half of Tuesdayâs argument, most of the conservative justices seemed opposed to Harrisâ argument and looked likely to constrain the governmentâs ability to bring civil penalty claims in agency proceedings.

Chief Justice John Roberts, a George W. Bush appointee, suggested the government wanted to extend broad executive authority over immigration beyond the justification for its application.

Justice Neil Gorsuch, a Donald Trump appointee, questioned why the administration should be allowed to set up a whole court system to adjudicate H-2A claims when federal courts already exist to do so.

Harrisâ stark warnings seemed to give some of the justices pause.

âMs. Harris put a lot of chips on the table when she finished saying this would be quite destructive for the government if she lost,â Roberts remarked.

Sun Valleyâs arguments, however, appeared to sway even more opinions in the governmentâs favor. Robert Johnson, an attorney with the Institute for Justice, struggled to articulate the bounds of the employerâs arguments.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh, another Trump appointee, described Johnsonâs proposal as âat war with clarity.â Justice Samuel Alito, a fellow Bush appointee, said he was outlining a “hodgepodge opinion.â

The courtâs three liberals seemed broadly opposed to Sun Valleyâs arguments from the start. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, a Joe Biden appointee, said the employer was âfighting the realityâ of the H-2A programâs purpose to ensure farmworkers werenât coming in and undercutting domestic workers. Justice Elena Kagan, a Barack Obama appointee, said the employerâs argument would prevent the government from targeting immigration fraud.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor, also an Obama appointee, said Sun Valleyâs arguments would allow employers to treat workers badly and gamble on whether the Justice Department had enough lawyers to penalize everybody who violates the programâs rules.

After nearly two hours of arguments, Harris made a final push for compromise during rebuttal.

âI don’t like the prospect of losing,â Harris said. âI think that’s very obvious. I hope we don’t lose this case because of the consequences. But if you were looking to which poison is the least bad, I agree that the poison that’s the least bad is at least saying that we can impose penalties initially in adjudications and then have de novo review in Article III courts.â

#7536. Ninth Circuit rebuffs SpaceX bid to force arbitration of harassment claims

In a split decision, the appellate panel rejected SpaceX's argument that sexual harassment claims must meet federal pleading standards to avoid being sent to arbitration.

PASADENA, Calif. (CN) â The Ninth Circuit on Tuesday rejected SpaceX’s attempt to force eight fired employees to arbitrate their wrongful retaliation claims, finding the claims stem from their concerns about sexual harassment at Elon Musk’s rocket business.

In a split decision, the appellate panel upheld last year’s ruling by a trial judge in Los Angeles who had concluded that the Ending Forced Arbitration of Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment Act of 2021 (EFAA) applied to the employees’ claims and, as such, rejected SpaceX’s request to compel arbitration.

While SpaceX argued on appeal that the EFAA requires sexual harassment claims to be substantial enough to survive a motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim, the Ninth Circuit panel found the law only requires that the complaint describes conduct asserted to be a basis for a sexual harassment claim.

“Congress could have easily drafted the EFAA to require courts to send sexual harassment disputes to arbitration only when the complaint ‘fails to state a claim upon which relief may be granted’ or ‘fails to state facts which, if true, would constitute sexual harassment,’” U.S. Circuit Judge Michelle Friedland wrote for the panel.

The fact that Congress didn’t chose to adopt those readily available and apparent alternatives is strong evidence that Congress did not intend to import the federal pleading standard into the EFAA, the Barack Obama appointee added.

The eight employees were fired in 2022 after they send an open letter to SpaceX management to express their concern that Musk’s lewd social media posts normalized and encouraged sexual banter, sexual harassment, and gender discrimination at SpaceX, which at the time was still headquartered in Hawthorne, California.

“Musk knowingly and purposefully created an unwelcome hostile work environment based upon his conduct of interjecting into the workplace vile sexual photographs, memes, and commentary that demeaned women and/or the LGBTQ+ community,” they claim in their complaint first filed two years ago in Los Angeles County Superior Court and subsequently removed to federal court in LA.

One of the posts they cite in their lawsuit involves Musk announcing his idea to create a Texas university similar to MIT which he would call “TITSâ and where âDs [womenâs bra size] would get degrees,â accompanied by an altered photo rendering a rocket to appear to be a giant penis.

The plaintiffs say Musk ordered them to be fired soon after they circulated their open letter.

“We are delighted with the Ninth Circuitâs ruling,” Anne Shaver, an attorney for the plaintiffs, said in an email. “This well-reasoned decision not only vindicates the right of our eight clients to proceed in open court on their sexual harassment claims against Musk and SpaceX, it clarifies the appropriate pleading standard under the EFAA for all victims of sexual harassment.”

Representatives of SpaceX didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

While U.S. Circuit Judge Danielle Forrest, a Donald Trump appointee, joined Friedland in rejecting SpaceX’s appeal, U.S. Circuit Judge Eric Tung, also a Trump appointee, dissented and said the panel should have reversed the trial judge’s ruling.

According to Tung, his colleagues opened the door to disgruntled employees’ creating a sexual harassment dispute on frivolous grounds and thereby evading their arbitration agreements.

“Under the majorityâs test, a plaintiff can escape an arbitration agreement if his complaint so much as purports to allege a sexual harassment dispute,” Tung wrote. “In other words, the majority accepts a plaintiffâs bare legal assertion, no matter how mistaken.”

#7535. Top Dallas County investigator arrested, charged with wife’s murder

Jimmy Harold Spurger Jr., 54, the chief investigator for the Dallas County public defender’s office, was arrested and charged with first-degree murder Saturday after his wife was found dead in their apartment. (Photo from the Dallas County Sheriff’s Department)

The chief investigator for the Dallas County public defender’s office was arrested and charged with first-degree murder Saturday after his wife was found dead in their apartment.

Jimmy Harold Spurger Jr., 54, who has worked for the public defender’s office for nearly 14 years, was married to his wife, Maria Teresa Spurger, for 35 years but filed for divorce in late October, according to Fox 4.

Local first responders who were conducting a welfare check Friday night forced their way into the apartment, where they found Spurger’s wife unresponsive on a couch with a knife in her neck, Fox 4 reports. Spurger also was found in the apartment, covered in blood and sitting next to a knife in the bedroom.

After responding officers found multiple pill bottles also covered in blood, they suspected that Spurger had ingested pills and transported him to the hospital, Fox 4 reports. He was later taken into custody and is being held on a $1 million bond.

Spurger has led the Investigative Division for the Dallas County public defender’s office for 11 months, Fox 4 reports. Previously, he spent more than 13 years in its Capital Murder Division. He also worked for more than 20 years in law enforcement, which included supervising investigations in the Child Abuse and Family Violence Division of the Dallas County district attorney’s office.

Dallas County Chief Public Defender Christi Dean told Fox 4 that Spurger was “an exemplary colleague,” and that “it’s hard to imagine that he has been charged with murder.”

“We know in our profession that the probable cause affidavit doesn’t tell the whole story,” Dean also reportedly said. “The media reports don’t tell the whole story. And we’re still in preliminary stages.”

Two months ago, Snow denied Maricopa Countyâs motion for relief from judgment. He agreed that the largest sheriff’s office in Arizona has come a long way since the days of Joe Arpaio, whose administration was found in a 2013 trial to have promoted a practice of racially profiling Latino drivers, but found it still has not achieved full compliance necessary to rid itself of a federal monitor.

In a Phoenix courtroom, Snow suggested better communication may help Sheridan, former chief deputy to Arpaio, turn a new leaf.

First, the county’s own traffic report data shows Hispanic motorists are still about 40% more likely to be arrested, stopped 30% longer and more than twice as likely to be searched compared to their white counterparts. Second, Sheridan has not yet eliminated a backlog of internal investigations into reports of civil rights violations.

Snow acknowledged that indicators of bias don’t necessarily mean policies or officers themselves are biased, but encouraged Sheridan to better explain to the plaintiff class and the public why else the bias shows up in the data.Â The judge also pushed Sheridan to take a more active role in those investigations.

Accepting that Sheridan wants to eliminate the backlog, Snow said he wonât yet hold the sheriff in contempt for being out of compliance, but he said issues regarding command structure and third-party investigators should be relatively easy to resolve.

Snow said heâs open to discussing what parts of his lofty orders may no longer require direct monitorship.

Sheridan didnât respond directly to Snowâs suggestions, but said it’s in the best interest of himself and the community that he comply with Snowâs orders.

âI involve myself in pretty much every aspect of compliance with the order,â he said.

Representing the sheriff, Joseph Popilizio of Jones, Skelton and Hochuli suggested the parties hold regular status conferences between already-established quarterly site visits to foster more open dialogue.

Snow emphasized that the community advisory board, established in 2013 to help the sheriff achieve compliance, should be part of those meetings.

The county has also held quarterly community meetings to hear from constituents directly, but Snow has seen them largely as a failure. He ordered the meetings be moved to the federal courthouse after an emotional July 2025 meeting got out of hand, then again ordered the meetings be virtual after attendees acted disrespectfully toward himself and members of the court-appointed monitoring team, which is made up of former police chiefs and county sheriffs.

Popolizio welcomed the community advisory boardâs participation in additional meetings.

Snow also warned Popolizio that some of his communications with the monitor, headed by former Rochester Police Chief Robert Warshaw, have violated Snow’s orders and âoften have an inappropriate tone.â

If the county or the sheriffâs office disagree with how the monitor implements Snowâs orders, the parties must first confer with the plaintiff class, represented by the American Civil Liberties Union of Arizona, before going to the monitor. Rather than argue with the monitor, Snow said Popolizio should then go directly to him if the monitor doesnât budge from there.

Popolizio agreed, but added that heâs been frustrated with the monitorâs own lackluster communication.

ACLU attorney Christine Wee agreed that more frequent communication would be helpful on all fronts.

The county has appealed Snowâs denial of its motion for relief. Still pending is the countyâs objection to the appointment of Shaneeda Jaffer as an independent investigator to review the sheriffâs own internal investigations. The county insists the sheriffâs office should maintain full authority over its own investigations.

Snow said he wonât require oral argument but will issue a ruling soon.

SAN FRANCISCO (CN) â Nima Momeni, a tech worker convicted of stabbing and killing Cash App founder Bob Lee beneath the Bay Bridge in San Francisco in April 2023, was sentenced Tuesday to 16 years to life in prison.

Presiding San Francisco Superior Court Judge Alexandra Gordon sentenced Momeni to 15 years to life in state prison, plus an additional year for a weapons enhancement. Once released, he will be on probation for the rest of his life.

A jury found Momeni guilty of second-degree murder in San Francisco Superior Court after a two-month trial in late 2024.

At trial, testimony and camera footage showed Lee and Momeni together the night of Leeâs killing in 2023. Prosecutors argued Momeni killed Lee in a fit of rage because Lee had been doing drugs with Momeniâs sister and introduced her to a drug dealer who sexually assaulted her.

In contrast, Momeni claimed he acted in self-defense and that Lee was on a bender of cocaine, alcohol and other substances that made him unstable and unpredictable in the days before the stabbing.

Before the sentence was handed down, Bob Leeâs brother Oliver Lee addressed the court, sharing memories of his brother and the pain his murder has caused the family.

âIâve been sitting through 19 days of trial watching [Momeni] take the stand to lie and tear down my brother while Bob was not there to answer,â he said. âHe got to call his mother; Bob got a 911 call.â

Oliver Lee also expressed gratitude to Gordon for tentatively imposing the maximum sentence in the case and thanked the jury, the San Francisco Police Department, and the district attorneyâs office for their work in the case.

âNo sentence brings back Bob. We have our family and our friends, and we are grateful for every one of them, but there will always be a piece missing,â he said.

Leeâs daughter, Scout Lee, also spoke, describing the day she found out her father was killed and the effect his death has had on her life.

âMy world did not just shift â¦ it shattered,â she said.

Standing alongside her grandfather and Bob Leeâs father, Scout Lee addressed Momeni several times in her statement.

âMr. Momeni, you have damaged me in no way a sentence can repair. Your cruel actions have â¦ consequences my family has to suffer for the rest of our lives,â she said.

âYou did not just end his life; you ended an entire future,â she added.

Momeniâs mother, Mahnaz Tayarani, spoke in support of her son, asking Gordon to consider who Momeni is as a whole person, describing him as ârespectful, hardworking and generous.â

âI humbly ask that you consider my sonâs sentence, you consider the complexities of this case, the depth of a motherâs love and that a personâs life can be more than the worst moment of his life,â she said.

Momeni also addressed the courtroom, acknowledging the âdeep sense of loss, pain and griefâ and insisting that he did not intend to cause any suffering.

âWhile we have completely different understandings of what happened â¦ I want you to know how truly sorry and regretful I feel for what both of our families have had to feel during this process,â he said.

Prior to sentencing, Gordon heard arguments on Momeni’s motion for a new trial based on supposed errors of law, prosecutorial misconduct and juror misconduct. After nearly two hours of arguments, Gordon denied the motion in a lengthy ruling from the bench.

Last March, Leeâs family filed a wrongful deathsuit against Momeniâs sister and mother in San Francisco Superior Court, claiming the family helped him cover up the murder. The suit is still ongoing.

Momeni additionally sued media outlets, including the LA Times, San Francisco Standard, and the New York Post, as well as photojournalist Paul Kuroda over the press coverage of his legal case, seeking $17 million in damages. A judge struck the lawsuit for failure to pay court fees this year.

#7532. Supreme Court agrees to weigh in on Goldman Sachs arbitration dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Friday afternoon added a new case to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term, granting a petition for review filed by Goldman Sachs Bank in a case over whether and when a bankruptcy court can override the Federal Arbitration Act and refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes.

The dispute in which the justices agreed to weigh in, Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown, began three years ago, when Rhea Brown and Gregory Maze filed for bankruptcy. Both listed credit card debts with Goldman Sachs Bank as one of their debts.

The Bankruptcy Code imposes an automatic stay, which (among other things) bars creditors from attempting to collect debts from someone who has filed for bankruptcy. Because Goldman Sachs, according to Maze and Brown, repeatedly continued to try to seek payment of their credit card debts, they filed an adversary proceeding (that is, a separate lawsuit within the broader bankruptcy case) against the bank, in which they contended that the bank had willfully violated the automatic stay provision.

Pointing to an arbitration clause in their credit card agreements, Goldman Sachs asked the bankruptcy court to put the adversary proceeding on hold and require Brown and Maze to arbitrate their dispute. The bankruptcy court denied that request, and both the federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld that ruling. A divided three-judge panel of the 4th Circuit concluded that requiring Brown and Maze to arbitrate their claim “would interfere and conflict with the strong and established policies and purposes of the Bankruptcy Code.”

Goldman Sachs came to the Supreme Court in June, asking the justices to take up its case. It told the court that the 4th Circuit’s ruling squarely conflicted with a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit. Moreover, it added, “[t]he practical stakes of these issues are enormous” because of the ubiquity of arbitration clauses in consumer credit agreements. The 4th Circuit’s decision, it said, “imperils the enforceability of arbitration agreements in many of them.”

After considering Goldman Sachs’ petition for review at four consecutive conferences, the justices granted it on Friday afternoon. The case likely will be argued sometime next year, with a decision to follow by late June or early July.

More orders from the justices’ private conference on Friday are expected at 9:30 a.m. EST on Monday.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7530. Jury convicts Virginia man of murdering, chopping up wife

Naresh Bhatt claims his wife died by suicide and that he panicked when he found her body, which led him to dismember her and throw her into the garbage.

MANASSAS, Va. (CN) âÂ A jury on Tuesday found a Northern Virginia man guilty on all counts related to murdering his wife, dismembering her body and stuffing it into a trash can.

After five weeks of trial, Naresh Bhatt, 39, of Manassas Park, listened Tuesday as a prosecutor implored jurors to convict him of murder in connection with the 2024 disappearance of Mamta Kafle Bhatt, 28, a nurse and the mother of the coupleâs now 3-year-old daughter. Her body was never found, but prosecutors charged her husband with defiling and concealing a body as well as murder.

While the case against Bhatt was circumstantial, he took the witness stand last week and denied that he killed her. Instead, he said that he found his wife’s body after she died by suicide. Fearing he would be blamed, he panicked and decided to chop up her body and toss it out with the trash.

“And now, the defendant wants you to believe his story, his made-up crazy story,” said Sarah Sami, senior assistant commonwealth’s attorney in Prince William County, Virginia, during closing arguments. “All the defendant has done that you’ve seen from the moment that Mamta went missing, all he did was lie.”

She told jurors Bhatt signaled his true intentions with a message sent to his wife in February 2024: “The days are coming that you’ll regret a lot.” Sami said, quoting the text message. “He told Mamta what he was going to do with her.”

He delivered on that promise 162 days later, according to prosecutors. “The defendant murdered Mamta Kafle,” Sami said, referring to the victim by her maiden name. ‘The defendant dismembered Mamta Kafle. And the defendant got rid of her like garbage."

Bhatt’s attorney Tracey Lenox, chief public defender for Prince William County, urged jurors to avoid doingÂ the “easy thing.” It would be easy, she explained, to “allow your instincts of compassion and empathy to dictate your discussion and decision-making when you go back to the jury room. The easy thing would be to give in to a gut level need. I think it is very human to place blame somewhere for the pain and the trauma that Mamta Kafle’s family has endured for the last two-plus years.”

Jurors, she said, should take care to determine only whether the prosecution has proven each element of the offenses beyond a doubt. This means the jury should not be in search of truth but “really inquisitors of doubt.”

Bhatt told his side of the story to a stunned courtroom. But when questioned by police after her disappearance, Bhatt initially said he didn’t know where his wife had gone. During closing arguments Tuesday, Lenox pointed out Bhatt says he actually told the suicide story two weeks after his arrest.

Mamta Kafle Bhatt’s mother, brother and a close collection of friends sat in the front row, mostly dressed in her favorite color â red. Beyond family, neighbors, fellow ex-patriots of Nepal, police investigators and nurses from area hospitals packed the courtroom.

Lindsay Clancy was being tried for first-degree murder. She admitted to killing her three children and claimed that she suffered from postpartum psychosis. (Photo by CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via the Associated Press)

Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse charged with strangling and killing her three small children in 2023, lost her bid to have her case dismissed Monday, setting the stage for a possible retrial.

Massachusetts Superior Court Judge William Sullivan’s 17-page ruling found that a retrial would not be considered double jeopardy because Clancy’s initial jury was deadlocked.

Clancy, 36, was on trial earlier this year for the strangling deaths of her three young children. The case ended in a mistrial after one juror, known as “Juror Doe,” held out for an acquittal. Clancy pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, alleging that she was undergoing postpartum psychosis at the time of the tragedy, according to coverage on Courthouse News Service.

Last week, a hearing seeking dismissal of the case explored the role of Michael Desronvil, who is referred to as “Juror Doe” in court records. Desronvil was accused of not following the court’s instruction.

Sullivan found that the evidence “did not reasonably suggest Juror Doe’s inability to deliberate or refusal to follow the law.”

On Nov. 2, the prosecution said it intends to try Clancy again. She initially faced three counts of murder for the deaths of Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months.

On Friday, the justices met in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. That afternoon, the Supreme Court announced that, during the conference, the justices added a new case to the oral argument docket: Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Today, the justices will hear arguments in two cases: Nielsen v. Watanabe, on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations; and Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., on whether the “just compensation” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires.

On Tuesday, the justices will hear argument in Department of Labor v. During oral arguments in November 2025, plaintiff attorney Amy Bellantoni told the Second Circuit that the city’s administrative constraints on gun purchasing âgo right to the very heart of the plain text of the Second Amendment, which is the right to keep and bear, to have and possess, and right to acquire is necessarily wrapped up within the right to possess, because without the ability to acquire, then you have no possession and no carriage, you have no defense.â

Regarding the waiting period, Bellantoni said the 5 to 15 minutes it takes to run the buyersâ background check would be sufficient.

#7521. Whose tradition, which history? Agency adjudication and Sun Valley Orchards

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Over the past few decades, several features of the administrative state have been subject to heated constitutional challenge. One of them is agency adjudication: the practice of resolving disputes “in-house” within administrative agencies instead of addressing these disputes directly in a court. Of late, the Supreme Court has applied a “history-and-tradition” methodology to assess the constitutionality of agency adjudication. But that methodology confronts the challenge of how to select from among multiple competing traditions the one that should carry the day. On Nov. 10, the court will hear a case, Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, that underscores the difficulties of carrying out its history-and-tradition methodology – difficulties that apply across many areas of law.

By way of background, the basic constitutional issue regarding administrative adjudication is as follows. Article III of the Constitution vests the “judicial power of the United States” in the Supreme Court and lower federal courts. From the founding and onward, however, disputes that fall within the jurisdiction of Article III courts have been heard in tribunals belonging to the other federal branches, such as territorial courts, military tribunals, bankruptcy courts, magistrate judges, and most pertinent for current purposes, administrative tribunals – for instance, by administrative law judges.

Agency adjudication of, say, Social Security and veterans’ benefits claims is an integral part of the administrative state. It provides a streamlined way of handling these claims and avoids clogging up the Article III courts. Although there is usually a right to appeal administrative determinations at some point to Article III courts, these courts apply a deferential standard of review.

The question arises whether administrative adjudication is compatible with the judicial scheme laid out in Article III of the Constitution. This is a practically significant issue; agency dispute resolution has substantial effects on individuals and companies, who can face considerable fines or penalties. To what extent, then, is agency adjudication outside Article III courts justified? And what kinds of limitations should be placed on it?

In the past few decades, the Supreme Court has turned to “history and tradition” to answer these questions. History and tradition as methods of constitutional interpretation are likely most familiar from cases on hot-button social issues, such as Dobbs (holding that there was no “history and tradition” of a right to have an abortion) and Bruen (holding that there was no “history and tradition” of requiring certain types of licenses to carry firearms outside the home). But the court has also drawn on history and tradition to shape the scope of federal judicial power, in contexts ranging from Article III standing to equitable remedies. One such setting is the division of labor between Article III courts and agency adjudicative bodies.

History and tradition play a dual role in the law of adjudication outside Article III courts. This pattern was on display in the Supreme Court’s 2024 case Securities and Exchange Commission v. Jarkesy, which addressed the constitutionality of agency adjudication of certain claims involving securities fraud. First, tradition provides a justification for non-Article III (including agency) adjudication of a limited class of claims deemed to involve “public rights,” that is, matters which historically “could have been determined exclusively by [the executive and legislative] branches.” In Jarkesy, the court listed “the collection of revenue,” “immigration,” “tariffs,” “relations with Indian tribes,” “the administration of public lands,” and “the granting of public benefits such as payments to veterans, pensions, and patent rights” as members of this class of claims. Since these matters, the court explained, historically could have been adjudicated outside Article III courts, they may be heard by non-Article III tribunals today.

Second, tradition provides a reason that claims involving “private” rather than “public” rights must be brought before Article III courts instead of administrative tribunals. A hallmark of a private-rights suit that belongs before an Article III court, the Jarkesy court stated, is being “made of the stuff of the traditional actions at common law tried by the courts at Westminster in 1789.”

In Jarkesy, the court decided that the securities fraud claim at issue resembled common-law fraud, a traditional common-law claim and so a private right requiring an Article III tribunal. (The court also emphasized that the remedy the SEC was pursuing – civil penalties – was historically enforceable in courts of law; accordingly, the SEC was bringing a suit “at common law” to which the Seventh Amendment jury trial right attached. Jarkesy thus revolved substantially around the jury trial right, which is not a question directly presented in Sun Valley.)

Tradition, then, helps to demarcate the boundary between claims that must be adjudicated by Article III courts (private rights) and claims that may be resolved before other courts, including administrative agencies (public rights). But how should the court decide whether a present-day claim fits into a tradition of private rights or public rights? In particular, what should the court do when there are multiple traditions into which a present-day claim might fit?

The court’s upcoming case Sun Valley provides an example of the problem of “too many traditions.” Sun Valley involves a nonimmigrant visa program, administered jointly by the Department of Labor and the Department of Homeland Security, that permits American employers to hire foreign laborers to perform temporary or seasonal agricultural work. As a condition of participating in the program, employers agree to provide certain workplace arrangements to both foreign and domestic workers. DOL found that Sun Valley, a New Jersey farm, had failed to provide these arrangements, and the agency assessed hundreds of thousands of dollars in civil penalties and back wages against Sun Valley. Sun Valley was required to contest these penalties before an administrative law judge, with deferential review by an Article III court. Sun Valley challenged the administrative-adjudication requirement as a violation of Article III, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit agreed with Sun Valley.

In Supreme Court briefing, the government and Sun Valley both appeal to the history-and-tradition methodology of Jarkesy, but they sharply disagree about which tradition is relevant. The government emphasizes traditions related to immigration. According to the government, its enforcement action fits within two historical categories of public rights adjudication that did not require Article III courts: rights “belonging to the sovereign, such as the right to determine whether to allow aliens into the country,” and “privileges conferred by the government, such as public benefits granted under government programs.” In the government’s view, Sun Valley violated the conditions of bringing foreign workers to the United States through an immigration program that offered the farm a benefit. The pertinent tradition is hence the history of adjudicating immigration- and benefits- related claims outside Article III courts.

Sun Valley, by contrast, casts its claim as akin to common-law breach of contract – a traditional private right requiring an Article III tribunal. DOL’s allegation, Sun Valley observes, was that Sun Valley had violated its agreement to provide certain working conditions to foreign and domestic workers. That allegation, Sun Valley contends, is simply a charge that Sun Valley breached a contract. Sun Valley further argues that DOL sought common-law remedies and in particular civil penalties – more evidence that the claim at issue involves a private right. To Sun Valley, the case is located outside the historical tradition of immigration adjudication because it is based on conditions of employment rather than immigration status. Consequently, it was unconstitutional for DOL to adjudicate Sun Valley’s dispute in-house.

Which party is right about the tradition into which the dispute over Sun Valley’s working conditions falls? Plausibly, the answer is “both.” Yes, the government is alleging that Sun Valley violated an agreement; but the agreement in question was concluded as part of an immigration program allowing Sun Valley to hire foreign workers.

So what are courts to do when, as here, they are faced with “too many traditions” – that is, traditions with different implications for the constitutional question at hand?

One possible response is to conclude that history-and-tradition analysis is hopelessly indeterminate and to reject this methodology. While many methods of constitutional interpretation fail to yield a single right answer, “history and tradition” is often justified precisely by its promise to produce constraint and fixity. Breaking this promise might be viewed as grounds for abandoning the history-and-tradition approach.

Complete repudiation of history and tradition, however, would be unwarranted. Historical practice has played an important role in both upholding and limiting non-Article III adjudication; it is a tool in judges’ toolbox and should not be thrown away.

Another option is to supplement history-and-tradition methodology, when it does not produce a clear result, with other modes of constitutional analysis. Earlier cases on non-Article III adjudication, for instance, appealed openly to practical considerations of government efficiency.

A third option would be to draw on other “modalities” of constitutional interpretation to inform the choice of which strand of tradition to emphasize. One such modality is precedent. Jarkesy did not directly confront a program like the DOL’s in Sun Valley, so it is not controlling precedent. But Jarkesy did seem to treat Congress’ broad power over immigration as a reason to uphold agency adjudication in immigration-related cases. Perhaps this suggests that DOL’s enforcement action fits better into a traditional public-rights than private-rights category.

The court may also decide to avoid the problem of too many traditions by taking a statutory “out.” When it took the case, the court added a question regarding DOL’s statutory authority to impose civil penalties and back wages on Sun Valley. The court may decide that DOL lacks such statutory authority, potentially by appealing to constitutional avoidance (in other words, construing the statute to grant DOL such authority would raise serious questions about the constitutionality of agency adjudication, which should be avoided unless necessary to decide). But the statutory question is not straightforward, and resolving it may well have ramifications for a wide array of agency-imposed penalties. At any rate, one or more of the justices can be expected to opine on Article III in Sun Valley, and the Article III issue is bound to recur.

Overall, the problem of “too many traditions” is by no means unique to the context of non-Article III adjudication. The Supreme Court faces challenging questions about how to apply history-and-tradition methodology when a present-day practice could plausibly fit into multiple traditions. The court’s response to these questions may have an important impact not only on the future of agency adjudication, but also on the trajectory of historically driven interpretation across a variety of pressing constitutional debates.

Rachel Bayefsky is Professor of Law at the University of Virginia School of Law, where she writes about civil procedure, constitutional law, and legal theory. She clerked for Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg in the 2018-2019 Term.

#7520. Law firm apologizes to truckers for ‘serial killer’ ad

A Texas law firm is apologizing for an ad in Maxim magazine that created such an outcry among truckers that truck stops pulled the publication from their shelves.

The full-page ad for San Antonio law firm Villarreal & Begum showed a picture of a truck cab beneath the words “serial killer.” Both the law firm and Maxim are apologizing for the ad after Pilot Flying J and TravelCenters of America pulled the magazine from their shelves. Publications with stories include HDT Trucking Info, TheTrucker.com, CSPNet.com, KIROTV.com and LandLinemag.com.

The copy read: “3,561 people died on America’s highways last year. Another 2.36 million were injured. You need a law firm you can Trust. You need Experience. You need Strength. You need Villarreal & Begum. We’re proven leaders in prosecuting cases involving death and catastrophic injury.”

In its statement, the law firm says it never intended “to disparage the hardworking Americans that drive tractor-trailers for a living. Our intent was to reach out to those individuals who have been involved in catastrophic accidents as a result of irresponsible drivers. The ad was inartfully created, and we could see how it may have caused our message to be misconstrued. We recognize the service that truck drivers provide to this nation and acknowledge that most truck drivers are safe and responsible drivers.”

Maxim also issued a statement saying the ad “does not reflect the beliefs or opinions of the people at this magazine, which recently has begun operating under new ownership.” The ad has been pulled from Maxim’s digital copy and replaced with facts about the trucking industry.

#7519. Fourth Circuit narrows government request for journalists’ LinkedIn records

The Fourth Circuit attempted to strike a balance between the need to protect national security and the need to protect the free press.

RICHMOND, Va. (CN) â The Fourth Circuit instructed a lower court Tuesday to narrow the amount of journalists’ records LinkedIn must turn over for an investigation.

âThe government sought and received a pair of orders to aid an investigation into the leaking of highly confidential military information to an unnamed news outlet.

âA lower court first granted the government’s request for a sweeping disclosure order under the Stored Communications Act requiring LinkedIn to produce records of journalists’ messages with confidential sources. The government sought journalists’ metadata records from an 18-month period, including their conversations with sources.

âThe lower court also granted a secrecy order that prohibited LinkedIn from telling its users about the disclosure for one year. U.S. Circuit Judge Harvie Wilkinson, a Ronald Reagan appointee, ruled that the orders were too broad.

â"It is part of the audacity of the American project to believe that collective security can coexist with individual freedom," Wilkinson said. “While we respect the government’s interest in gathering information potentially relevant to the leak, neither the Stored Communications Act nor the Constitution permit the district court to approve orders that, by all apparent indications, are substantially overbroad.”

âWilkinson disagreed with the government’s argument that LinkedIn failed to identify an injury. Wilkinson reasoned that the orders may cause the platform reputational and financial harm.

â"Confidentiality of sources is the lifeblood of a free press," Wilkinson said.

âOver a billion people use LinkedIn, including 94% of American journalists, according to a 2022 Pew Research Center survey.

â"Through the aid of LinkedIn, a journalist and source can therefore find each other and exchange extensive information without ever establishing any publicly visible connection," Wilkinson said. “Without the ability to communicate privately that LinkedIn offers, that would be impossible.”

âThe court sealed many details of the investigation, including which news outlet shared the confidential information. The government described the subject article as revealing a top-secret United States military operation in a foreign country. The government’s attorney, Joshua Ferrentino, described the investigation as unusual during a September hearing.

âWilkinson denied LinkedIn’s motion to quash the disclosure order in its entirety. Wilkinson emphasized the life-and-death nature of the confidential information the news outlet shared.

“Leaks of classified materials can transmit highly sensitive information to our adversaries in areas in which stealth is essential,” Wilkinson said. “Such leaks can also place in greater danger the lives of the men and women working in covert operations to protect our country.”

âStill, Wilkinson acknowledged the role the press plays in American society.

â"When a free press reports on the operations of government, it will often be the case that reporting exposes matters that the government might wish undisclosed, either to save itself from embarrassment or because it simply prefers to have its actions unexamined," Wilkinson said. “This does not confer upon government the right to silence.”

âLinkedIn moved to narrow the secrecy order so it could inform a lawyer for the news outlet of the disclosures. A magistrate judge denied the motion to modify the orders, ruling that the Stored Communications Act allows platforms to challenge orders only on logistical grounds. The magistrate judge further ruled that the government’s request was not overbroad because it is typical that records requests encompass some records unrelated to the criminal investigation.

â"While some degree of overbreadth may be inevitable, the SCA and the Constitution require the district court to analyze the degree of overbreadth and trim the more far-fetched reaches of the government’s records request," Wilkinson said.

âAttorneys representing LinkedIn and the government did not return a request for comment. U.S. Circuit Judges Andrew Wynn, a Barack Obama appointee, and Nicole Berner, a Joe Biden appointee, concurred with Wilkinson.

#7516. Court declines to hear dispute tied to George Floyd protests and cases involving former baseball player Roberto Clemente and actor Randy Quaid

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Monday denied review in over 200 cases, including a dispute that arose in Minneapolis after the murder of George Floyd in police custody in 2020 and clashes involving actor Randy Quaid and the sons of a baseball legend. These denials were part of a list of orders from the court’s Nov. 6 conference that was released on Monday morning.

The court on Friday granted one petition for review from that conference, in a case involving whether and when a bankruptcy court can refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes.

The Minneapolis case was brought by a group of businesses located at the intersection where Floyd was killed. Following Floyd’s death, the city blocked the intersection “with concrete barricades,” which “prevented vehicles and pedestrians from accessing” the area, and withdrew police protection, according to the businesses’ petition for review. Those barricades remained in place “for over one year,” and led to significant economic losses for the businesses and a surge in violent crime, the petition said.

The businesses challenged the city’s actions in state court, alleging that it had violated the Constitution’s takings clause and similar protections in Minnesota’s constitution by interfering with their operations and failing to compensate them accordingly. However, a district court and the Minnesota Court of Appeals disagreed, and the Minnesota Supreme Court denied the businesses’ request for it to review the case.

In August, the businesses came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to revive their case. On Monday, the Supreme Court declined to do so without comment.

The case involving family members of baseball legend Roberto Clemente also involved the takings clause. Clemente’s adult sons and companies associated with preserving Clemente’s legacy challenged Puerto Rico’s use of the baseball legend’s image on “license plates and tags,” an initiative that “generat[ed] 15 million dollars for Puerto Rico” but also fueled ill will against the family, “who Puerto Ricans thought were to blame for a fee levied on them during dire economic times,” according to the petition for review. Through their lawsuit, the Clementes aimed to block Puerto Rico from using their father’s image in the future and recover financial damages.

Earlier this year, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit prevented the Clemente family’s takings clause claim from proceeding, emphasizing that it (along with the federal statute concerning trademark law) is “designed not to protect legacies but instead to remedy ... the taking of property for public use without just compensation.” In June, the Clementes asked the Supreme Court to take up the case and, among other things, clarify that the takings clause can apply in cases involving intangible property.

After considering the petition at three consecutive conferences, the justices on Monday denied review.

In Monday’s order list, the justices also asked the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on AstraZeneca UK Ltd. v. Atchley, a case on whether U.S. terrorism victims may sue 21 “of the world’s largest pharmaceutical and medical-device companies” under the Antiterrorism Act for allegedly aiding and abetting terrorists in Iraq.

Additionally, the justices sent Roybal v. Griffith, a transgender female inmate’s challenge to jail policies in El Paso County, Colorado, regarding the treatment of transgender inmates back to the lower court for reconsideration in light of West Virginia v. B.P.J. and United States v. Skrmetti.

In B.P.J., the court ruled in June that state laws barring transgender female athletes from participating on women’s and girls’ sports teams do not violate a federal civil rights law or the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment. In Skrmetti, the court last year upheld a Tennessee law prohibiting some medical treatments for transgender minors, holding that it was not subject to heightened scrutiny under the equal protection clause.

Also on Monday, the justices granted the solicitor general’s request to participate in three oral arguments during the December argument session:

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7514. Giving and Receiving: Adoption attorney often on road donates building to legal services group for children

Lawyers sometimes take unusual paths to the profession, but adoption lawyer Robert Noone’s was inspired by men of the cloth. After attending St. Mary’s Seminary in Baltimore, he was helping an order of Jesuits assist the residents of Appalachia with community organizing and voting issues. The priests encouraged Noone to enter law school instead of the priesthood because they thought he could better advocate for social change as an attorney.

To support himself through West Virginia University College of Law, he played guitar in bars. After graduating in 1983, he did labor law and personal injury work at Crandall & Pyles, and by 1989 he decided to open his own firm, Robert Noone Legal Services, where he represented children as a guardian ad litem in abuse and neglect cases and as a juvenile defense attorney with cases that ranged from truant kids to kids who kill. He also handled some adoption cases in West Virginia. He now focuses on adoption services in West Virginia and Alabama.

In 2024, he signed over the deed to his 5,000 square-foot building in Logan, West Virginia, and renovated the building for its new tenant. and this month, ChildLaw Services Inc.—a statewide nonprofit law firm that exclusively works with children by offering life skills and educational programs and legal help for juvenile defense, guardianships and other services—moved in. The nonprofit law firm named the building the Noone ChildLaw Center for Children and Teens.

ChildLaw helped Noone with his work over the years, and he later became a “virtual lawyer”—performing almost everything online and meeting people by video, at their homes or inside local fast-food restaurants. He plans to continue adoption work without an office.

“He has always had a love and heart for children, so we’ve teamed up over the years on projects. He’s been a good friend,” says Monica Holliday, ChildLaw Services’ executive director.

Where you really considering becoming a priest?

Yeah, let's not say that loud. I'd been in a minor seminary, then a college seminary and then getting ready to go into theology. The Catholic education back in the liberal days, they tell you to question everything. And I think I questioned myself right out of a religion. And I went to work with the Jesuits.

Why after making partner at Crandall & Pyles did you decide to start your own firm?

I had a judge tell me: “Bob, I've watched you for a while. It's time for you to, you know, venture out on your own.” And that gave me confidence. And, you know, a lot of encouragement from friends. And what I would not want to write down, though, in a labor law firm, I was probably paid less than my secretary.

Is it true you wear the hats of both an airplane pilot and the Rev. Bob Noone, officiating marriages, including same-sex weddings?

I would meet people at airports and perform them there, but also I did a lot just in my office. I wanted people to feel that it was not just a “drive-by” wedding. Or “fly-by,” as the case may be. I always made them tell me their love story, and I would shape the vows from what I learned. That was fun when the South was so resistant to change. … Now acceptance of LGBTQ has gotten better here.

You worked as a guardian ad litem during your career and then decided to just focus on the legal work around adoptions. Why?

You get to that point. Where you hear your last sad story: that mother who wouldn't see her kid because, oh, she forgot to go pee in a jar. And I hit that point a few years back, and I decided I'm just going to help put kids in homes.

You are a music lover and have been in many bands as a performer. But you have a story about a young lady who was skipping school who also, you discovered, had some hidden musical talent.

This would have been around 2009. I was doing a lot of juvenile work then, and she was truant. I said, “What do you do for fun?” And she was big. She quit going to school because she was so overweight. And she said, "Well, I love to sing." I’m thinking she would name Pink or Gwen Stefani or one of these people. She goes, “Aretha Franklin.” Well, she did great. But the real kicker was, I said, “If you go to school”—this was in like April—"the next two months without missing, you'll get to sing with my band, Daddy Rabbit."

How many adoptions have you helped with over the years?

When I count all those I supervise—I have two lawyers now that work with me—probably a little over 2,000.

In West Virginia last week, there's one point the three of us may be in four or five different counties in one day. People thought after 43 years, I'm giving a building away, I'm retiring. Hell to the no! I'm only 69, people. There's a lot of music left to play, cases to argue.

What kinds of challenges do you help navigate for people wanting to adopt?

In West Virginia, we do our same-sex adoptions, but we also do adoptions for people that aren't married. You know, just to clarify, because [the law] says a single parent can adopt or a married couple—husband and wife—but it doesn't say a single parent. And Alabama, in fact, passed a law that specifically forbids two single people from adopting. Go figure that out.

#7512. Supreme Court allows Trump administration to continue border wall construction

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume construction of a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. In a four-page, unsigned opinion, the justices granted the government’s request to pause an order by a federal district judge that had temporarily halted the project. Only Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that she would have denied the government’s request.

The dispute began earlier this year, when then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, issued three waivers of various environmental and conservation laws to authorize construction of the wall in the Big Bend region, which includes parts of Big Bend National Park. Noem and Mullin relied on a provision of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 that gives the DHS secretary the power to “waive all legal requirements” necessary “to ensure expeditious construction” of border walls and roads. When they announced the waivers, Noem and Mullin indicated that the Big Bend area “is an area of high illegal entry” requiring additional walls and barriers.

A group of plaintiffs opposed to the construction – an environmental group, a local landowner who works as a river guide, and a group formed to preserve a church – went to federal court to challenge the waivers’ legality. On Oct. 2, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone temporarily barred the Department of Homeland Security from continuing construction on the border wall in the Big Bend region “until and unless” the government complies with environmental and other applicable laws.

In a written opinion that she released on Oct. 14, Cardone reasoned that the challengers were likely to prevail on their claim that the DHS secretary did not have the authority to issue the waivers. She relied on the major questions doctrine – the idea that if Congress intends to give a federal agency the power to make decisions of vast economic or political significance, it must say so very clearly. In particular, she emphasized, the Big Bend region is not an area with a high number of illegal entries. To the contrary, she stated, although it “comprises over 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border,” it makes up only a tiny percentage (“between 0.3% and 2.2%”) of the migrants apprehended while crossing the border. Therefore, she wrote, “if the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector, and the waiver authority would apply to the entire U.S.-Mexico border. If that were the case, Congress could have simply authorized construction ‘to deter illegal crossings.’” The major questions doctrine instructs courts to avoid “interpretations that would render limiting language meaningless,” Cardone concluded.

After Cardone declined to pause her ruling to give the government time to seek Supreme Court review, the Trump administration came to the Supreme Court, where it asked the justices not only to temporarily freeze Cardone’s order but also to grant review and summarily (that is, without additional briefing or oral argument) reverse it. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued that Cardone lacked the power to consider the challengers’ claim based on the major questions doctrine because their complaint specifically alleged that the DHS secretary “lacked ‘clear congressional authorization’ … to issue the waivers” under the IIRIRA – which, he said, was a statutory claim that “Congress denied district courts” the authority “to entertain.” But in any event, Sauer continued, even if the DHS secretary’s power to issue waivers under IIRIRA “implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the Secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction.”

The challengers urged the justices to leave Cardone’s order in place. Eric Glitzenstein, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs, told the justices in a 40-page filing that if her order were paused or lifted, it would permit the Trump administration to “immediately resume blasting, bulldozing, road construction, and other border barrier-related construction across one of the most remote and ecologically and culturally significant landscapes in the United States.”

The challengers argued that the major questions doctrine applied to their claim. They emphasized that the DHS secretary’s “decision to waive myriad federal, state, local, and tribal laws across vast geography for the purpose of building border infrastructure, even through national and state parks where border crossings are miniscule, is a truly ‘extraordinary’ assertion of power.” Because Congress “did not clearly authorize the sweeping exercise of power asserted here,” they wrote, the government’s “actions therefore amount to a constitutional violation of the major questions doctrine.”

In Monday’s opinion, the justices denied the government’s request to summarily reverse Cardone’s ruling but granted its request to put it on hold. “The Government,” the court explained, “is exceedingly likely to prevail on its argument” that Cardone did not have the power to consider the challengers’ “so-called major-questions-doctrine claim.” That claim, the court emphasized, contends only “that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority,” which is not a constitutional claim. This is true, the court continued, even if the challengers rely on the major-questions doctrine, because that doctrine is a rule used to interpret laws. “There is no such thing as a ‘constitutional’ major-questions claim.”

The other factors that courts normally consider in deciding whether to pause a lower court’s decision also point in the government’s favor, the justices said. For example, Cardone’s order “delays the Government’s construction of border barriers and roads in the Big Bend Sector” and, as a result, “impedes the Government from advancing its ‘compelling interests’ in border security and integrity.” Moreover, the government is suffering permanent harm from the costs – “nearly half a million dollars … per day” – that it is incurring while the construction is on hold, but which cannot be recovered. Finally, the court wrote, “[t]he Government’s interest … outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by” the challengers.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7509. Border wall decision caps busy Monday at SCOTUS

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

It was a busy Monday at the Supreme Court: the justices heard two oral arguments, released an order list, and decided the border wall dispute on the interim docket. Keep reading to catch up on these and other developments.

On Monday, the Supreme Court granted the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that she would deny the request. Learn more about the dispute in the On Site section below.

Earlier on Monday, the justices heard arguments in two cases: Nielsen v. Watanabe, on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations; and Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., on whether the “just compensation” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires.

Also on Monday, the Supreme Court denied review in over 200 cases, including disputes involving the George Floyd protests in Minneapolis, actor Randy Quaid, and the sons of former baseball player Roberto Clemente. It also asked the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a case over whether U.S. terrorism victims may sue 21 pharmaceutical and medical-device companies under the Antiterrorism Act for allegedly aiding and abetting Iraqi terrorists. For more on Monday’s order list, see the On Site section.

Today, the justices will hear argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC, on whether the Constitution allows the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – to adjudicate an employer’s obligation to comply with employment agreements concerning temporary immigrant workers.

On Wednesday, the Supreme Court Building will be closed in recognition of Veterans Day.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

#7506. Justices dubious of fee award in eminent domain dispute about interstate pipeline

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The argument yesterday in Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc. left little doubt about how the justices will resolve this one: they seem unlikely to hold that the gas company condemning land for a federally approved pipeline should have to pay attorneys’ fees that the United States would not have to pay if it condemned the land directly.

The dispute involves the 1947 Natural Gas Act’s treatment of interstate natural-gas pipelines. When the federal government approves such a pipeline, the Natural Gas Act allows it to acquire the land in which to build the pipeline or leave that to the gas company. In either case, if the landowner does not agree, a suit exercising the federal government’s right of eminent domain can force a transfer of the land for a “necessary right-of-way,” so long as the landowner receives the “just compensation” that the Fifth Amendment requires when property is “taken for public use.”

The landowners here argue, with some support in the lower courts, that if the pipeline company rather than the United States condemns the land, the pipeline company should be bound by state-law rules that require more compensation than the federal Constitution. In particular, North Dakota law well might require the company to pay the attorneys’ fees of the landowners.

The justices, though, were having none of it. The air was redolent with skepticism from the moment Robert McNamara rose to press the landowners’ view. Justice Clarence Thomas started off by asking – doubtfully – whether “if the U.S. delegates its power … of eminent domain, you’re saying that it brings with it state law trappings of just compensation?” Chief Justice John Roberts quickly interjected that “it seems to me it’s just a more efficient process to have a private developer get the land under the same terms as the federal government without having to pay the attorneys’ fees that the state wants to insist on.” When McNamara stuck to his position, the chief justice eventually concluded the discussion by commenting: “I don’t understand why this isn’t an easy case.”

It seemed for a while that several of the justices would offer a slightly different reason to reject McNamara’s argument, with Justice Sonia Sotomayor coming in quickly to press the idea that “you’re trying to separate the right to eminent domain from the right to compensation, correct?” and then pointing to “a[n] 1893 case … in which we said, [it is] a settled principle of universal law that [they are] inseparably connected. … I don’t see how your separation of these principles honors that.”

For Ketanji Brown Jackson, the problem was McNamara’s assumption “that state law, with respect to just compensation is the default,” and that “it needed to be ousted by congressional expression.” But if that were true, she pointed out, why would Congress have thought it important, in a 1946 condemnation statute adopted just one year before the Natural Gas Act, to take the trouble explicitly to import state law? That statute’s treatment of the condemnation problem appears to contrast sharply with the treatment in the Natural Gas Act just one year later. As Jackson asked pointedly: “What is [that language] doing there if … silence [by Congress means that] state law applies?” Justices Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett pressed McNamara on the same point: they took it as self-evident that the 1946 statute importing state law suggested that a 1947 statute silent on the topic calls for the application of the baseline federal rule emphasized by Thomas and Roberts.

You have to expect it will be pretty hard to fashion a majority if Justice Thomas and the chief justice on one side see it as an “easy case” against you and Jackson and Sotomayor on the other side are predisposed to reject what you have to say. And nothing in the remainder of the argument suggested any reason to think otherwise. The presentations of Paul Hughes (for the pipeline company) and Zoe Jacoby (for the government) were filled for the most part with softball questions speculating about why lower courts might have found such an obvious question challenging.

I would not be at all surprised if this was one of the very first decisions from the November session. The share of simple unanimous statutory cases is not so high as it used to be, but this has all the earmarks of a straightforward unanimous affirmance.

Ronald Mann is a professor of law at Columbia, where he teaches courses in commercial finance, payment systems and deals.
